process.label: Order of the work
process.gloss: The same fifty-one stations regrouped by the operation each one stages, in the order of Ripley's twelve gates: calcination first, projection last. The road does not move; only the reading does.

groups.label: Calcination

groups.label: Solution

groups.label: Separation
groups.gloss: dividing the subtle from the gross, the pure from the impure

groups.label: Conjunction
groups.gloss: the marriage of the separated principles, male to female

groups.label: Putrefaction
groups.gloss: the blackening death in the sealed vessel, without which nothing generates

groups.label: Congelation
groups.gloss: the fixing of what was volatile into a stable white body

groups.label: Fixation
groups.gloss: making the volatile abide the fire and no longer fly

groups.label: Digestion
groups.gloss: the long gentle heat in which the matter feeds on itself

groups.label: Fermentation
groups.gloss: leavening the stone with gold, as bread is leavened

groups.label: Multiplication
groups.gloss: increasing the virtue of the stone in quantity and in strength

groups.label: Projection
groups.gloss: the casting of the finished stone upon the base metal

emblem-00.discourse: Maier's introductory apparatus presents Atalanta Fugiens as an exercise in multi-sensory pedagogy: the subtitle promises emblems for the eyes, fugues for the ears, and epigrams for the intellect, engaging sight, he a ring, and reason simultaneously in the pursuit of Nature's secrets. The myth of the footrace serves as a heuristic model for the reader's own engagement — just as Hippomenes must distract the swift Atalanta with golden apples to win the race, the reader must use the sensory enticements of image, music, and verse to catch the fleeting truths of alchemical philosophy. De Jong characterizes this as Maier's 'lusus serius' or serious game, a Renaissance pedagogical strategy in which play, meditation, and intellectual pursuit are fused into a single practice of discovery. The frontispiece thus functions not merely as decoration but as an instruction manual for how to read the fifty emblems that follow — each a puzzle requiring the reader to chase meaning across multiple registers.
emblem-00.image_description: The title-page engraving depicts the race of Atalanta and Hippomenes at the bottom, with Hippomenes in mid-stride casting a golden apple while Atalanta stoops to retrieve one from the ground. At the left margin, Venus extends the golden apples to Hippomenes; at the right, the couple embraces in a temple entrance before emerging behind it as a lion and lioness, their transformation by Cybele. The upper register shows Hercules in his lion-skin approaching the tree of the Hesperides, reaching for the golden fruit while the three Hesperides — Aegle, Arethusa, and Hespertusa — watch from above. The central cartouche frames the title text in an architectural surround, unifying the mythological scenes into a single emblematic program that introduces the work's central conceit.

commentary.title: Atalanta
commentary.body: Maier makes Atalanta the titular figure of his entire work, drawing on Ovid's Metamorphoses X to allegorize the volatile mercurial principle as a swift maiden who can only be overtaken through cunning rather than force. De Jong demonstrates that Atalanta's flight structures the allegorical logic of all fifty emblems, each of which dramatizes some aspect of the pursuit between volatile and fixed.

commentary.title: Hippomenes
commentary.body: Maier casts Hippomenes as the alchemical adept who must use strategy and the golden apples of Art to slow and fix the fleeing volatile principle. De Jong reads the golden apples as the catalytic agents of the Work, without which brute pursuit of Mercury would be futile, making Hippomenes a figure for the disciplined application of alchemical knowledge.

commentary.body: First Rosicrucian manifesto (1614), announcing the Brotherhood of the Rose Cross and calling for a universal reformation of knowledge through alchemy and spiritual illumination.

commentary.title: Hercules
commentary.body: Hercules appears on the AF frontispiece reaching for the golden apples of the Hesperides. Forshaw identifies him as Maier's archetype of the alchemist — the hero who uses both strength and cunning to obtain the fruit of immortality (the philosopher's stone). His lion-skin connects him to the alchemical lion symbolism that recurs throughout the fifty emblems.

commentary.title: Cybele
commentary.body: Cybele appears on the AF frontispiece where the transformation of Atalanta and Hippomenes into lions is depicted. The couple embraces in her temple entrance before emerging behind it as lion and lioness. Forshaw notes that Cybele's chariot is traditionally pulled by lions, connecting the mythological punishment to the alchemical symbolism of the winged and wingless lions that recur throughout the emblem series.

motto.la: Nutrix ejus terra est
motto.en: The wind carried it in its belly.

epigram.en:
Romulus is said to have been nursed at the coarse udders of a wolf,
And Jupiter to have been nursed by a goat, and these facts are said to be believed:
Should we then wonder if we assert
That the earth suckles the tender Child of the Philosophers with its milk?
Maier, Examen Fucorum Pseudo-Chymicorum, 41:
If an insignificant animal nursed such great heroes,
Shall not the Terrestrial Globe be a nurse?

emblem-01.discourse: Maier develops the Tabula Smaragdina's declaration that 'the wind carried it in its belly' into an extended analogy between alchemical generation and natural gestation. He argues that the philosophical substance must first be conceived in air (the volatile spirit) before being nourished by earth (the fixed body), just as an embryo is carried in the womb before being nursed after birth. The discourse draws on Peripatetic natural philosophy to assert that nourishment must share the nature of what it feeds, establishing the principle that the Stone requires earth — that is, a fixed, corporeal substrate — as its nurse. Maier cites Hermes Trismegistus as the ultimate authority for this teaching.
emblem-01.image_description: A muscular male figure, identified as Boreas the North Wind, strides across a rocky landscape carrying a swaddled infant against his torso. The wind god's hair and drapery stream behind him, and billowing clouds fill the sky above. Below, a female earth figure — massive, globular, with exposed breasts — reclines on the ground, her body merging with the landscape itself. A small child nurses at her breast while animals graze nearby, establishing the maternal earth as nurse.

sources.name: Tabula Smaragdina (Emerald Tablet)
sources.gloss: The Tabula Smaragdina, or Emerald Tablet, is a brief Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus that circulated widely in Latin translation from the twelfth century onward, encoding the foundational principle that operations in the macrocosm mirror those in the microcosm. De Jong (1969) demonstrates that Maier deliberately derives the mottos of Emblems I and II from the Tabula's dictum that the earth is the nurse of the philosophical child, establishing the Hermetic cosmological framework as the opening gesture of Atalanta Fugiens. These two emblems anchor the entire work in the tradition

commentary.title: Tabula Smaragdina
commentary.body: The Emerald Tablet; foundational Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. 'As above, so below' cosmology.

commentary.title: Prima Materia
commentary.body: Maier treats prima materia as the hidden substrate underlying the entire emblem sequence, the formless potential that must be identified and worked upon before any transformation can begin. De Jong shows that Maier draws on both Aristotelian hylomorphism and the Turba's teachings on primary matter, particularly in the opening emblems where the cosmological framework is established.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The undifferentiated base substance from which the Stone is made; paradoxically described as worthless and everywhere available, yet unrecognized by the ignorant.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The radical moisture or fundamental bodily substrate that precedes differentiation into the four humors; the basic vitality underlying all physiological processes.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The raw, unformed psyche before the work of individuation begins; the chaotic prima materia of the unconscious from which the Self must be extracted.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The primordial chaos or hyle from which God fashioned the cosmos; the formless substrate underlying all manifest creation, coeval with the Creator.

commentary.title: Opus Magnum
commentary.body: Maier conceives Atalanta Fugiens itself as a guide to the Opus Magnum, with the fifty-emblem sequence mapping the stages of the Work from cosmological foundation through purification, conjunction, and final perfection. De Jong argues that the deliberate ordering of emblems reflects the sequential logic of the Great Work, making the book a symbolic enactment of the alchemical process it describes.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Great Work itself: the entire sequence of operations from prima materia to Philosopher's Stone, encompassing nigredo, albedo, citrinitas, and rubedo.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The complete course of treatment from diagnosis through crisis to cure; the physician's magnum opus of restoring the patient from sickness to perfected health.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The lifelong work of self-transformation; the soul's journey from unconscious chaos through successive purifications to the gold of realized wisdom.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The divine creative act mirrored in human artifice; the alchemist's work as a microcosmic recapitulation of God's original creation of order from chaos.

commentary.title: Ceres
commentary.body: Maier invokes Ceres in connection with the nursing and nourishment imagery of the opening emblems, where the earth as nurse sustains the philosophical child. De Jong reads the agricultural goddesses in AF as figures for the receptive, fertile matter that nourishes the seed of gold toward its maturation.

commentary.title: Boreas
commentary.body: Boreas is the central figure of Emblem I, visualizing the Emerald Tablet's teaching. Forshaw identifies him as Mercury/quicksilver in the Pseudo-Lullian tradition of argent vive. His two sons (red-haired and white-haired) represent Sulphur and Quicksilver. The Ritman Library's 17th-century painting pairs this first emblem with the last (Emblem L), suggesting the work's circular structure.

motto.la: Nutrix ejus terra est
motto.en: Its nurse is the Earth.

epigram.en:
Romulus is said to have been nursed at the coarse udders of a wolf,
And Jupiter to have been nursed by a goat, and these facts are said to be believed:
Should we then wonder if we assert
That the earth suckles the tender Child of the Philosophers with its milk?
If an insignificant animal nursed such great heroes,

emblem-02.discourse: Maier continues the the me of Emblem I, now emphasizing that the earth is specifically the nurse, not the mother, of the philosophical substance. He distinguishes between generation (which occurs through the volatile principle, the wind) and nourishment (which requires the fixed, earthy body). The discourse argues that just as human food must be converted into the substance of the body it feeds, so the alchemical earth must be assimilated into the growing Stone. Maier draws a careful analogy between the stages of infant feeding — blood in utero, milk after birth, solid food later — and the progressive fixation of the volatile philosophical substance.
emblem-02.image_description: The same globular earth-mother figure from Emblem I reappears at center, her body forming a living landscape with a small child nursing at her breast. She sits or reclines against a hillside with a town visible in the distance. Animals — a cow and smaller creatures — graze at her feet, reinforcing her identification with the nurturing earth. The composition emphasizes the maternal relationship between the vast earthly body and the tiny philosophical infant.

The composition emphasizes the maternal relationship between the vast earthly body and the tiny philosophical infant.

commentary.title: Maier's discourse
commentary.body: Maier continues the the me of Emblem I, now emphasizing that the earth is specifically the nurse, not the mother, of the philosophical substance. He distinguishes between generation (which occurs through the volatile principle, the wind) and nourishment (which requires the fixed, earthy body). The discourse argues that just as human food must be converted into the substance of the body it feeds, so the alchemical earth must be assimilated into the growing Stone. Maier draws a careful analogy between the stages of infant feeding — blood in utero, milk after birth, solid food later — and the progressive fixation of the volatile philosophical substance.
commentary.cite: Summary of Maier's prose discourse (Claudiens corpus extraction)

commentary.title: De Jong's analysis
commentary.body: Retort (artificial) and nature work together. Art serves Nature as teacher.
commentary.cite: H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems (1969), Emblem II section

commentary.title: Historical commentary
commentary.body: Notes the pregnant female with terrestrial globe as 'nurse of tender child.'
commentary.cite: Walter Pagel, Review of H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1973), Review discussion

commentary.title: Historical commentary
commentary.body: Pagel identifies Emblem II's pregnant female figure with the terrestrial globe as symbolizing the earth as 'nurse of the tender child of the Philosophers', tracing its iconographic tradition to Albertus Magnus' Philosophia pauperum (1493) and Mylius' Philosophia reformata (1622).
commentary.cite: Walter Pagel, Review of H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1973), p. 102

commentary.title: Alchemical text referenced
commentary.body: The Tabula Smaragdina, or Emerald Tablet, is a brief Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus that circulated widely in Latin translation from the twelfth century onward, encoding the foundational principle that operations in the macrocosm mirror those in the microcosm. De Jong (1969) demonstrates that Maier deliberately derives the mottos of Emblems I and II from the Tabula's dictum that the earth is the nurse of the philosophical child, establishing the Hermetic cosmological framework as the opening gesture of Atalanta Fugiens. These two emblems anchor the entire work in the tradition

commentary.title: Tabula Smaragdina
commentary.body: The Emerald Tablet; foundational Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. 'As above, so below' cosmology.

commentary.title: Prima Materia
commentary.body: Maier treats prima materia as the hidden substrate underlying the entire emblem sequence, the formless potential that must be identified and worked upon before any transformation can begin. De Jong shows that Maier draws on both Aristotelian hylomorphism and the Turba's teachings on primary matter, particularly in the opening emblems where the cosmological framework is established.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The undifferentiated base substance from which the Stone is made; paradoxically described as worthless and everywhere available, yet unrecognized by the ignorant.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The radical moisture or fundamental bodily substrate that precedes differentiation into the four humors; the basic vitality underlying all physiological processes.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The raw, unformed psyche before the work of individuation begins; the chaotic prima materia of the unconscious from which the Self must be extracted.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The primordial chaos or hyle from which God fashioned the cosmos; the formless substrate underlying all manifest creation, coeval with the Creator.

commentary.title: Ceres
commentary.body: Maier invokes Ceres in connection with the nursing and nourishment imagery of the opening emblems, where the earth as nurse sustains the philosophical child. De Jong reads the agricultural goddesses in AF as figures for the receptive, fertile matter that nourishes the seed of gold toward its maturation.

commentary.title: Distillatio
commentary.body: Maier incorporates distillation within the broader complex of purificatory operations depicted in the washing and heating emblems, where volatile spirits are separated from dense matter and recollected in purified form. De Jong connects this to the practical apparatus referenced in Emblem II's retort imagery.

motto.la: Vade ad mulierem lavantem pannos, tu fac similiter
motto.en: Go to the woman who washes the sheets and do as she does.

epigram.en:
Go to the woman who washes the sheets and do as she does.
She moistens the dirty linen with warm water;
Imitate her, and you will not go wrong in your art.
For the water washes the blackness from the body,
And what was stained by dirt becomes white through repeated washing,
Drenched by rain, dried by sun-warmth.

emblem-03.discourse: Maier argues that the alchemical purification process mirrors the everyday work of washing dirty linen: just as earth-stains on fabric are removed by water and then dried by sun and wind, so the impurities of the philosophical substance must be cleansed through repeated washing and exposure to the elements. The discourse develops the principle that what comes from earth is cleaned by the next element in the sequence — water purifies earth, air dries what water has cleaned. Maier presents the was her woman as a figure for the alchemist who must patiently repeat the cycle of dissolution and drying, an operation the tradition calls the albedo or whitening stage.
emblem-03.image_description: A woman kneels beside a wooden washing trough in an outdoor setting, scrubbing sheets or linens in soapy water. Her sleeves are rolled up and her posture suggests vigorous labor. A second figure, likely the alchemist-observer, watches from nearby. In the background, linens hang on a line to dry against a landscape of trees and buildings. The scene is emphatically domestic and practical, grounding the alchemical process in the imagery of common housework.

readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: Washing represents all purification processes. Removal of black (nigredo), purification to white (albedo). Medical connection to Saturn's melancholy. Relates to dyeing techniques where bleaching precedes dyeing.

commentary.title: Albedo
commentary.body: Maier figures the whitening primarily through washing imagery in Emblem III, where the laundress bleaching sheets represents the purification of matter from its blackened state. registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The whitening: purification of the black mass through washing and sublimation, yielding a pure white earth or powder—the stage of purificatio.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Restoration of phlegmatic balance; the cleansing of corrupt humors and return to a state of bodily purity, analogous to convalescence.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: Illumination after the dark night: the purified soul perceives spiritual light, achieving clarity and the dawn of higher consciousness.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Moon's dominion; the reflective feminine principle that receives and transmits celestial light, associated with silver and nocturnal dew.

commentary.title: Calcination
commentary.body: Maier subsumes calcination within the broader washing metaphor of Emblem III, where the laundress's work represents all purificatory operations including burning away impurities. De Jong notes that Maier treats calcination not as an isolated laboratory step but as part of a symbolic cluster linking washing, bleaching, and the removal of the black (nigredo) from impure matter.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Heating the base matter to extreme temperatures to reduce it to powder or calx, driving off volatile components and exposing the fixed salt.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The burning away of disease and corrupt matter; cauterization and the application of intense remedial heat to purge infection.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The burning away of ego-attachments and worldly illusions; the trial by fire that strips the soul down to its essential, incombustible core.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The action of celestial fire on terrestrial matter; the solar principle's consuming power that reduces gross forms to their elemental substrate.

commentary.title: Tinctura

registers.label: in the heavens

motto.la: Conjunge fratrem cum sorore et propina illis poculum amoris
motto.en: Join brother and sister and give them the cup of love.

epigram.en:
From her own father, Myrrha received the beautiful Adonis.
As a marriage of brother and sister they unite:
Give them the cup of love, let them drink,
And bring forth from the work of their union
A nobler offspring than was ever produced
By the embraces of Mars and Venus.

emblem-04.discourse: Maier frames the alchemical coniunctio as a marriage between brother and sister — the masculine and feminine principles of the same substance — who must be united by the 'cup of love,' the solvent that dissolves both into a single new body. He draws on Oedipus's unwitting marriage to his mother Jocasta as an analogy for the paradoxical union of opposites that share a common origin. The discourse argues that the philosophical work is fundamentally gendered labor: the masculine role is to beget and govern, the feminine to conceive and nourish. Maier cites both classical mythology and Arabic alchemical sources to establish that this conjunction of fixed and volatile is the central operation of the entire art.
emblem-04.image_description: A young man and woman face each other in a formal garden or courtyard setting, joining hands or exchanging a cup between them. Their postures suggest both greeting and ceremonial union. Behind them, architectural elements frame the scene — an archway or portico. The composition centers on the gesture of joining, with the cup of love serving as the mediating object between the two figures.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: Brother (hot, dry, choleric) = Fire. Sister (cold, moist, phlegmatic) = Water. Union of contrasts per Empedocles. Related to Emblems XXXIX (Oedipus/mother), XLI (Myrrha/father), XLIV (Osiris/Isis).

readings.author: Hereward Tilton
readings.title: The Quest for the Phoenix: Spiritual Alchemy and Rosicrucianism in the Work of Count Michael Maier (1569-1622)
readings.text: Tilton identifies the 'philothesia' in epigram 4 as a love potion offered at the Saturnalia. The brother-sister conjunction and nectar cup connect to Maier's Rosicrucian enigmas in Symbola Aureae Mensae, linking alchemical marriage to the fraternity's invitation.

commentary.title: Coniunctio
commentary.body: Maier presents the union of opposites as the central mystery of the Work, depicting it through the marriage of brother and sister (Emblem IV) and the hermaphrodite figure (Emblem XXXIII). De Jong traces this theme across 14 emblems, identifying it as the structural backbone of the entire emblem sequence.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The chemical wedding of Sulphur and Mercury—the union of the red king and white queen in the sealed vessel to produce the hermaphroditic Rebis.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The rebalancing of contrary humors into harmonious proportion; the therapeutic union of hot and cold, moist and dry principles within the body.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The sacred marriage of opposites within the psyche—conscious and unconscious, masculine and feminine—producing wholeness and inner unity.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The conjunction of Sol and Luna, the great celestial marriage whose earthly reflection governs generation and the harmony of macrocosm and microcosm.

commentary.title: Regina
commentary.body: Maier pairs the Queen with the King as the feminine lunar counterpart necessary for the coniunctio, appearing in the marriage and union emblems where male and female principles must join. De Jong reads the Queen as Maier's figure for the receptive mercurial principle that completes the King's solar fixity.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The White Queen: philosophical Mercury, the lunar-feminine principle whose volatile, moist nature must be fixed and united with the Red King to complete the work.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The receptive, nourishing aspect of the body's economy; the phlegmatic-sanguine balance that sustains fertility, moisture, and regenerative capacity.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The soul's receptive wisdom; the feminine principle of intuition and contemplation that complements and completes the active masculine will.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Moon as cosmic consort; the reflective, generative, and cyclical principle that receives solar light and transmits it to the sublunary world.

motto.la: Appone mulieri super mammas bufonem, ut ablactet eum, et moriatur mulier, sitque bufo grossus de lacte
motto.en: Put a toad to the breasts of a woman, that she may suckle it, and the woman may die and the toad grow big from the milk.

epigram.en:
Put a cold toad at the breast of a woman,
So that it may drink from the source of milk like a child.
Let it swell into a large growth,
And let the woman become ill and die.
Make a noble medicine from it,
Which drives the poison out of the human heart and takes away destruction.

emblem-05.discourse: Maier frames the alchemical operation as gendered labor, arguing that the masculine principle be gets and governs while the feminine conceives, bears, and nourishes. He develops the toad as a figure for the volatile, poisonous agent that must be fed by the maternal body of the prima materia — a feeding that kills the nurse but matures the product. Maier draws the analogy to Cleopatra's death by asp-venom, suggesting that the transfer of vital essence from woman to toad mirrors the fixation of the volatile sulphur through prolonged contact with a liquid menstruum. The discourse cites the Pseudo-Aristotelian Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis as the source of this toad-nursing imagery.
emblem-05.image_description: A woman sits outdoors on a stone bench, her bodice loosened, nursing a large toad at her breast. The toad clings to her chest with its forelimbs, drawing milk while the woman's expression registers calm resignation rather than horror. Behind her, a walled town rises against a hilly landscape with scattered trees. In the foreground, a second smaller toad waits on the ground. The scene inverts the conventional nursing Madonna into an image of productive destruction.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: Four stages: decomposition, purification, formation into pliable substance (woman dies, toad grows), hardening into stone. Toad = earth, Woman = water. One nature coagulates only through dissolution of another. Catena Aurea linking microcosm to macrocosm.

commentary.title: Maier's motto
commentary.body: Put a toad to the breasts of a woman, that she may suckle it, and the woman may die and the toad grow big from the milk.
commentary.latin: Appone mulieri super mammas bufonem, ut ablactet eum, et moriatur mulier, sitque bufo grossus de lacte

commentary.title: Maier's epigram
commentary.body:
Put a cold toad at the breast of a woman,
So that it may drink from the source of milk like a child.
Let it swell into a large growth,
And let the woman become ill and die.
Make a noble medicine from it,
Which drives the poison out of the human heart and takes away destruction.
commentary.cite: Maier's own verse for this emblem, in translation

commentary.title: What the plate shows
commentary.body: A woman sits outdoors on a stone bench, her bodice loosened, nursing a large toad at her breast. The toad clings to her chest with its forelimbs, drawing milk while the woman's expression registers calm resignation rather than horror. Behind her, a walled town rises against a hilly landscape with scattered trees. In the foreground, a second smaller toad waits on the ground. The scene inverts the conventional nursing Madonna into an image of productive destruction.

commentary.title: Maier's discourse
commentary.body: Maier frames the alchemical operation as gendered labor, arguing that the masculine principle be gets and governs while the feminine conceives, bears, and nourishes. He develops the toad as a figure for the volatile, poisonous agent that must be fed by the maternal body of the prima materia — a feeding that kills the nurse but matures the product. Maier draws the analogy to Cleopatra's death by asp-venom, suggesting that the transfer of vital essence from woman to toad mirrors the fixation of the volatile sulphur through prolonged contact with a liquid menstruum. The discourse cites the Pseudo-Aristotelian Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis as the source of this toad-nursing imagery.
commentary.cite: Summary of Maier's prose discourse (Claudiens corpus extraction)

commentary.title: De Jong's analysis
commentary.body: Four stages: decomposition, purification, formation into pliable substance (woman dies, toad grows), hardening into stone. Toad = earth, Woman = water. One nature coagulates only through dissolution of another. Catena Aurea linking microcosm to macrocosm.
commentary.cite: H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems (1969), Emblem V section

commentary.title: Philosopher's Stone
commentary.body: Maier presents the Stone not as a single emblem but as the telos toward which the entire fifty-emblem sequence converges, with the geometric formula of Emblem XXI and the mutual destruction of Emblem L both pointing to its achievement. De Jong argues that Maier understands the Lapis as the perfected union of fixed and volatile, achieved through the complete cycle of dissolution and reconstitution.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Lapis Philosophorum: the perfected red powder or tincture capable of transmuting base metals into gold and serving as the universal medicine—the opus's ultimate product.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The panacea or universal medicine that cures all diseases, restores youth, and grants extraordinary longevity—the supreme aim of iatrochemical practice.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The fully realized self; the incorruptible inner gold achieved through the complete integration of all psychic opposites—the goal of the soul's Great Work.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The quintessence crystallized: the fifth element that transcends and perfects the four mundane elements, embodying the perfection of cosmic order in material form.

commentary.title: Coagulation
commentary.body: Maier illustrates coagulation most vividly in Emblem V, where the toad grows large from the woman's milk as one nature solidifies through the dissolution of another. De Jong traces this reciprocal logic to the Pseudo-Aristotelian and Lullian traditions, showing that Maier understood fixation and dissolution as inseparable complementary operations.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The fixing and solidifying of volatile matter into stable form; the dissolved components reunite into a new, permanent body—the Stone.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The restoration of firm bodily substance from dissolved or weakened states; the clotting and consolidation that restores structural integrity.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The embodiment of spiritual insight in stable, lived practice; the crystallization of illumination into enduring character and wisdom.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The cosmic principle by which formless potentiality congeals into manifest creation; the earth-principle that gives permanence to celestial influences.

commentary.title: Dissolution
commentary.body: Maier frames dissolution as both destructive and generative, from the woman's death in Emblem V to the mutual annihilation of dragon and woman in Emblem L. De Jong identifies the final emblem's return to primary matter as the culminating dissolution that completes the Work, drawing on the Turba's teaching that all creation begins in liquefaction.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Dissolving the calcined matter in the mercurial water; the body is liquefied so that its hidden seed may be released from the fixed matrix.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The therapeutic dissolving of calcified obstructions and hardened humoral deposits; restoring fluidity to the body's circulatory economy.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The dissolution of rigid psychic structures; the letting go of fixed identities and beliefs that obstruct the flow of inner transformation.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: Water's primordial action on earth; the lunar solvent that returns differentiated forms to the undifferentiated ocean of potentiality.

commentary.title: Catena Aurea
commentary.body: Maier invokes the golden chain in the context of Emblem V to articulate the continuous link between microcosmic and macrocosmic processes of transformation. De Jong reads this as Maier's expression of the Hermetic principle that alchemical transmutation participates in a cosmic hierarchy extending from base matter to the divine, with each stage of the Work mirroring a corresponding celestial operation.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The golden chain: the unbroken sequence of transmissions linking ancient sages to present practitioners, guaranteeing the authenticity of alchemical knowledge.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The chain of medical authority from Hippocrates through Galen to Paracelsus; the lineage of healing wisdom transmitted from master to student across centuries.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The unbroken chain of initiatic transmission; the living lineage connecting the seeker to the original source of esoteric knowledge through teacher-student succession.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: Homer's golden chain linking heaven to earth: the vertical axis of emanation by which divine influence descends through the planetary spheres to terrestrial matter.

commentary.title: Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis
commentary.body: Short Latin alchemical treatise falsely attributed to Aristotle, transmitted through the Artis Auriferae compilation. Source for elemental union imagery.

commentary.title: Ars Magna
commentary.body: The combinatorial art attributed to Ramon Llull, adapted by pseudo-Lullian alchemists into a framework for understanding dissolution and coagulation as reciprocal operations.

commentary.title: Solutio
commentary.body: Maier figures solutio through the imagery of drowning, melting, and immersion that recurs across the emblem sequence, where solid forms must be returned to liquid before they can be reconstituted in perfected form. De Jong connects this to the Turba's teaching that the Work begins in liquefaction.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The dissolving of solid matter into liquid form using the philosophical mercury; the body must be reduced to its primordial water before reconstitution.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The liquefaction of hardened deposits and obstructions in the body; restoring the natural flow of humors through dissolution of morbid concretions.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The melting of the hardened heart; emotional release and the surrender of rigid ego-structures to the transformative waters of the unconscious.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The universal solvent principle, the action of the primordial waters from which all forms originally emerged and to which they cyclically return.

commentary.title: Solve et Coagula
commentary.body: Maier encodes the solve et coagula rhythm throughout Atalanta Fugiens, from the reciprocal dissolution-coagulation of Emblem V to the final mutual destruction of Emblem L. De Jong identifies this alternating pattern as the structural principle governing the progression of the entire emblem sequence.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The fundamental axiom: dissolve the fixed and coagulate the volatile. All alchemical operations reduce to this rhythm of breaking down and reconstituting matter at a higher level.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The therapeutic cycle of breaking down diseased structures and rebuilding healthy tissue; the alternation of catabolism and anabolism that sustains bodily renewal.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The universal rhythm of spiritual growth: dismantling old beliefs and identities (solve) and crystallizing new understanding into lived wisdom (coagula).

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The cosmic pulse of creation: the eternal alternation between dissolution into chaos and reconstitution into order that drives the cyclical life of the universe.

commentary.title: Apocalyptic Woman / Turkish Madonna
commentary.body: While the Apocalyptic Woman appears in the Symbola Aureae Mensae rather than directly in the Atalanta Fugiens, Szulakowska argues that the same sacramental theology underlies both works. AF Emblem XL's two fountains are identified as Maier's most overt reference to the alchemical Eucharist — the elixir of life described as analogous to 'the water of life of Christ, meaning both Baptism and the Eucharist.' The nursing motif in AF Emblem V connects to the lac virginis tradition.

motto.la: Seminate aurum vestrum in terram albam foliatam
motto.en: Sow your gold in the white foliated earth.

epigram.en:
The farmers entrust their seed to the fat earth,
After having foliated it with the ploughshare;
Sow your gold in the white foliated earth,
Which will yield you fruit with interest.
If you do this, you will rejoice in a rich harvest,
When the grain has multiplied in good soil.

emblem-06.discourse: Maier develops an extended agricultural analogy: just as the farmer must sow grain in prepared soil to reap a harvest, the alchemist must 'sow' philosophical gold in 'white foliated earth' — a specially prepared mercurial substrate — to produce the Stone. Drawing on Plato's division of the civic body into physicians and farmers, Maier argues that the alchemist combines both roles, healing metals while cultivating them. The discourse establishes a key principle: the seed (gold) must be of the same species as what it produces, and the earth (mercury) must be receptive and properly tempered. The white, foliated quality of the earth indicates the albedo stage, where the purified substrate is ready to receive the active seed.
emblem-06.image_description: A farmer figure kneels in a plowed field, sowing seed from a bag or pouch into furrows of white or pale earth. The field is carefully tilled in neat rows, and the landscape behind shows a cultivated countryside with distant buildings and trees. The emphasis falls on the act of sowing — the careful placement of precious material into prepared ground — with the whiteness of the earth itself visually prominent.

commentary.title: Albedo
commentary.body: Maier figures the whitening primarily through washing imagery in Emblem III, where the laundress bleaching sheets represents the purification of matter from its blackened state. De Jong connects this to the sowing of gold in white foliated earth (Emblem VI), establishing albedo as the preparatory ground for the final reddening.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The whitening: purification of the black mass through washing and sublimation, yielding a pure white earth or powder—the stage of purificatio.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Restoration of phlegmatic balance; the cleansing of corrupt humors and return to a state of bodily purity, analogous to convalescence.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: Illumination after the dark night: the purified soul perceives spiritual light, achieving clarity and the dawn of higher consciousness.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Moon's dominion; the reflective feminine principle that receives and transmits celestial light, associated with silver and nocturnal dew.

commentary.title: White Lead
commentary.body: Maier uses white lead in Emblem VI as the purified substrate into which gold must be sown, drawing an extended analogy between agricultural cultivation and the alchemical work. De Jong identifies this as Maier's image for the product of the albedo stage, the white foliated earth that serves as the receptive ground for the final reddening and multiplication of the Stone.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Plumbum album or cerussa: the whitened form of lead, an intermediate product signaling partial purification on the way from Saturn's darkness to lunar silver.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Used in traditional pharmacopoeia as a desiccant and cooling agent for inflamed wounds, despite its known toxicity—a dangerous remedy requiring careful dosage.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The partially purified soul: no longer in the blackness of nigredo but not yet fully illuminated; the intermediate stage of spiritual convalescence.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The transition from Saturn (lead) toward Luna (silver); the liminal zone between planetary influences where base matter begins to receive celestial whiteness.

commentary.title: Sol
commentary.body: Maier consistently identifies Sol with gold and the masculine fixed principle throughout Atalanta Fugiens, particularly in Emblem VI where gold must be sown in white foliated earth and in the frontispiece where Hippomenes carries golden apples. De Jong demonstrates that Maier's Sol operates simultaneously as metal, planet, and philosophical principle.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Gold in its philosophical sense: the perfect, incorruptible metal whose seed must be extracted and multiplied to produce the Philosopher's Stone.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The heart as the body's sun; the vital center radiating life-giving warmth and sanguine vitality to every organ through arterial circulation.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The illuminated consciousness; the divine spark or inner gold that the Great Work seeks to reveal beneath the dross of unrefined nature.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Sun as sovereign of the planetary hierarchy; source of all light, heat, and generative power in the macrocosm, father of the alchemical dyad.

commentary.title: Multiplicatio
commentary.body: Maier treats multiplication as the final operation following the achievement of the Stone, extending the agricultural metaphor of Emblem VI where sowing gold in white earth yields an abundant harvest. De Jong reads the multiplication as Maier's figure for the self-propagating nature of the perfected Stone, which can transmute quantities far exceeding its own mass.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The augmentation of the Stone's potency through repeated cycles of dissolution and coagulation, increasing its power to transmute ever greater quantities of base metal.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The amplification of a remedy's efficacy through careful preparation and potentiation; a small quantity of perfected medicine healing many patients.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The multiplication of spiritual gifts: as the adept's realization deepens, its transformative influence radiates outward to benefit others.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The principle of cosmic abundance: from the One proceed the many; the fecundity of nature that generates infinite diversity from a single divine seed.

commentary.title: Fermentatio
commentary.body: Maier treats fermentation as the vivifying operation that brings the nearly completed Stone to life, analogous to the leavening of bread or the action of a seed in prepared earth. De Jong connects this to the agricultural metaphors of Emblem VI, where the ferment of gold activates the receptive white earth to produce the final multiplication.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The leavening of the white stone with a small quantity of gold or its ferment, initiating the final transformation toward the Red Tincture.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Analogous to the digestive ferment that transforms food into nourishment; the vital leaven that activates the body's regenerative processes.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The catalytic encounter with a living spiritual tradition or teacher that activates latent potential; the yeast of grace working in the soul.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The generative ferment implanted by the Creator in all of nature; the seminal principle that drives cosmic becoming and the multiplication of forms.

commentary.title: Latona
commentary.body: Maier uses Latona in Emblem VI as a figure for the impure matter that must be washed and whitened before gold can be sown in it. De Jong connects the name Latona to the alchemical term laton (impure alloy), making her a mythological personification of the base material awaiting purification through the albedo.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: An imperfect body composed of Sol and Luna, as Bonus describes: she must be whitened (dealbate Latonem) by washing with Mercury to reveal the hidden gold and silver within.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The diseased or impure body harboring latent health; the patient whose mixed condition contains the seeds of both sickness and cure.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The soul burdened by unresolved contraries; the mother of Apollo and Diana who suffers persecution until her divine children—light and reflection—are born.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The material world pregnant with celestial potential; the earthly matrix from which solar and lunar principles must be separated and purified by the art.

commentary.title: Aurum Philosophicum
commentary.body: Maier consistently distinguishes between common gold and philosophical gold throughout Atalanta Fugiens, particularly in Emblem VI where the gold sown in white earth is the seed of the philosophical rather than the metallic variety. De Jong traces this distinction to the Rosarium tradition where philosophical gold is the product of art perfecting nature.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Philosophical gold: not common bullion but the perfected seed of gold freed from material impurity—the active principle of the completed Stone.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The perfected vital essence; potable gold as the supreme medicine that restores perfect health by harmonizing all bodily processes to their ideal state.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The incorruptible core of the self; the imperishable spiritual gold that survives every trial and constitutes the philosopher's true attainment.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The solar substance in its purest form; the celestial gold that corresponds to the Sun's essence rather than its mere terrestrial reflection in mineral veins.

commentary.title: Aqua Regia
commentary.body: Maier references the concept of a universal solvent capable of dissolving even gold within the broader dissolution imagery of Atalanta Fugiens. De Jong connects this to the alchemical paradox that the most noble substance requires the most powerful agent of destruction before it can be reconstituted in perfected form.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The royal water: a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold—the only solvent powerful enough to attack the noblest metal.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: A corrosive remedy of extreme potency, used in minute doses to dissolve calcified obstructions that milder treatments cannot address.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The supreme solvent of ego: a crisis or ordeal so powerful it dissolves even the most fixed and defended aspects of the personality.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The primordial deluge or universal solvent; the catastrophic dissolution that reduces even the most permanent cosmic structures to their elements.

motto.la: Fit pullus ab ovo volans, qui iterum cadit in nidum
motto.en: A young bird flies up from the nest and falls back into the nest again.

epigram.en:
The eagle had built a nest in a hollow rock,
In which it hid and fed its young:
One of them, trying to fly, fell back into the nest,
For the feathers were not yet fully grown.
The bird rises again, and falls back, until
Its wings have grown strong enough to sustain flight.

emblem-07.discourse: Maier describes a species of bird that flies upward from its nest only to fall back again repeatedly, developing this as an analogy for the alchemical process of sublimation and condensation. He argues that the volatile philosophical substance must be repeatedly driven upward (sublimated) and allowed to fall back (condensed) until it is sufficiently matured to sustain it self. The discourse connects this to the broader principle that Nature works through cyclical repetition rather than linear progress. Maier suggests that the bird's eventual success in flight corresponds to the moment when the volatile spirit is finally fixed and can maintain its elevated state.
emblem-07.image_description: A young bird — identified in the motto as a philosophical chick — launches upward from a nest perched in a tree or rocky outcrop, wings spread in attempted flight. Below, the same or another bird falls back toward the nest, unable to sustain its ascent. The landscape includes trees and possibly a distant town. The dual image of rising and falling captures the cyclical nature of sublimation and descent.

readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: Winged = volatile/Mercury/Moon/female. Wingless = fixed/Sulphur/Sun/male. Elements bonded despite contrasts. Phoenix symbolism: resurrection through fire and dissolution.

sources.name: Senior Zadith (Muhammad ibn Umail), Tabula Chimica
sources.gloss: The Tabula Chimica is a Latin translation of an alchemical work by the tenth-century Arabic author Muhammad ibn Umail, known in the Latin West as Senior Zadith, whose visionary imagery profoundly influenced medieval and early modern alchemical symbolism. De Jong (1969) traces the winged and wingless bird motif of Emblem VII directly to Senior's text, where the two birds represent the volatile (Mercury) and fixed (Sulphur) principles that must be bonded despite their contrasting natures. Emblem VII's depiction of the young bird flying from the nest and falling back encodes this teaching in Maie

sources.name: Lambsprinck, De Lapide Philosophico
sources.gloss: Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico is a late sixteenth-century alchemical emblem book that pairs symbolic engravings with verse explanations, establishing a visual tradition of alchemical emblems upon which Maier builds. De Jong (1969) and Pagel (1973) both identify Lambsprinck as a prototype for Maier's method of encoding alchemical doctrine in pictorial form, with Emblem VII's winged and wingless bird imagery drawing on a shared symbolic vocabulary. Lambsprinck's work thus represents a key link in the genealogy of the alchemical emblem tradition that culminates in Atalanta Fugiens.

De Jong (1969) identifies it as the direct motto source for Emblems IV and V, providing both the brother-sister marriage imagery (the union of hot/dry and cold/moist principles) and the striking image of the toad suckling at the woman's breast. These two emblems draw their central conceit of elemental union through mutual transformation directly from the Pseudo-Aristotelian

sources.name: Merlini Allegory
sources.gloss: The Merlini Allegory is a medieval alchemical narrative in which a king suffering from a wasting disease is cured through a sequence of purgative and transformative operations, serving as an extended parable for the purification of base metal. De Jong first analyzed this source in his 1964 article on Emblem XLVIII and expanded the treatment in his 1969 monograph, demonstrating that Maier draws the entire King Duenech narrative from this tradition. Emblem XLVIII depicts the king accepting a curative potion, with the medical-humoral allegory encoding the alchemical process of purging impurities

commentary.title: Mercurius
commentary.body: Maier encodes Mercurius as the volatile, fleeing principle throughout Atalanta Fugiens, most explicitly in the frontispiece where Atalanta herself represents the volatile Mercury that Hippomenes (Sulphur) must pursue and fix. De Jong shows that the winged figures in Emblems VII and XVI consistently signify the Mercurial principle in its lunar, feminine aspect.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The philosophical Mercury: not common quicksilver but the universal solvent and volatile principle—the moist, cold, feminine component of the metallic dyad.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The vital spirit or pneuma that circulates through the body; the mercurial principle governing nerve function, respiration, and the subtle fluids.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The anima or world-soul; the mediating spirit that connects body and soul, matter and intellect—Hermes as psychopomp guiding transformation.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The planet Mercury as cosmic messenger between Sun and Moon; the principle of mediation and communication linking all levels of the great chain of being.

commentary.title: Sulphur
commentary.body: Maier consistently figures Sulphur as the fixed, pursuing principle, embodied in the frontispiece by Hippomenes who chases Atalanta with golden apples as catalytic lures. De Jong demonstrates that the wingless figures in Emblems VII and XVI represent Sulphur's solar, masculine nature, which must bond with its volatile counterpart to complete the Work.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The philosophical Sulphur: the hot, dry, masculine, combustible principle in metals—the active seed that gives form and color to the metallic body.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The vital heat or innate calor that drives digestion, growth, and generation; the choleric fire that, in proper measure, sustains bodily life.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The soul's desire and will; the active, formative principle of consciousness that shapes raw experience into meaning and purpose.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The solar and fiery principle; Sulphur corresponds to the Sun's generative heat that activates all earthly matter through its formative rays.

commentary.title: Sol
commentary.body: Maier consistently identifies Sol with gold and the masculine fixed principle throughout Atalanta Fugiens, particularly in Emblem VI where gold must be sown in white foliated earth and in the frontispiece where Hippomenes carries golden apples. De Jong demonstrates that Maier's Sol operates simultaneously as metal, planet, and philosophical principle.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Gold in its philosophical sense: the perfect, incorruptible metal whose seed must be extracted and multiplied to produce the Philosopher's Stone.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The heart as the body's sun; the vital center radiating life-giving warmth and sanguine vitality to every organ through arterial circulation.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The illuminated consciousness; the divine spark or inner gold that the Great Work seeks to reveal beneath the dross of unrefined nature.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Sun as sovereign of the planetary hierarchy; source of all light, heat, and generative power in the macrocosm, father of the alchemical dyad.

commentary.title: Luna
commentary.body: Maier figures Luna as the volatile, feminine counterpart to Sol, embodied in the fleeing Atalanta of the frontispiece and the winged figures of Emblems VII and XVI. De Jong traces Maier's lunar symbolism to the Senior Zadith tradition, where Moon and Sun must unite to produce the perfected Stone.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Silver in its philosophical sense: the receptive, reflective metal that must be conjoined with Sol to achieve the complete work.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The brain and lymphatic system; the cool, moist, phlegmatic principle governing the body's receptive and reflective capacities.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The receptive, contemplative faculty of the soul; the mirror that reflects divine light without generating it—imagination and intuition.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Moon as cosmic mediator between celestial fire and terrestrial water; governess of tides, menstruation, and all cyclical change in the sublunary world.

commentary.title: Fixatio
commentary.body: Maier presents fixation as the essential counterpart to volatilization throughout Atalanta Fugiens, encoding it in the frontispiece narrative where Hippomenes must capture and fix the fleeing Atalanta. De Jong identifies the pursuit-and-capture motif as Maier's master allegory for the fixation of Mercury by Sulphur, the operation without which the Stone cannot be achieved.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Rendering volatile matter stable and resistant to fire; the spirit is permanently bound to the body so it can no longer escape through heating.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The stabilization of volatile symptoms and humoral imbalances; making a cure permanent rather than merely suppressing recurring disease.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The permanent anchoring of spiritual realization in embodied life; ensuring that transcendent insight does not evaporate when the adept returns to daily existence.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The principle of cosmic fixity: the immovable center around which the celestial spheres rotate, the axis mundi that grounds the turning heavens.

commentary.title: Tabula Chimica
commentary.body: Latin translation of an alchemical work by Muhammad ibn Umail (Senior Zadith), containing visionary imagery of volatile and fixed principles as paired birds.

motto.la: Accipe ovum et igneo percute gladio
motto.en: Take the egg and pierce it with a fiery sword.

epigram.en:
There is a bird in the world, more sublime than all,
Whose egg to search for is your only care.
A soft white surrounds the yellow yolk;
Strike it cautiously with a fiery sword, as is the custom.
Let Mars lend his aid to Vulcan: the chick thence arising
Shall be the conqueror of iron and fire.

emblem-08.discourse: Maier develops the egg as a figure for the sealed vessel containing the prima materia, arguing that it must be pierced — that is, opened to the action of fire — with a fiery sword to release and transform its contents. The discourse draws on the widespread alchemical tradition of the philosophical egg (ovum philosophicum), where the shell represents the vessel, the white the mercury, and the yolk the sulphur. Maier argues that the sword of fire must be applied with precision — too little heat fails to open the egg, too much destroys the embryonic substance within. The operation described is calcination, the controlled application of heat to break down the initial form of the material.
emblem-08.image_description: A hand extends from the left holding a flaming sword, driving it into a large egg that sits on a surface or pedestal at center. The egg cracks under the blade's impact, and flames or vapors escape from the breach. The setting is minimal, focusing attention entirely on the violent yet precise act of piercing the philosophical egg. The fiery sword introduces the element of controlled heat into the self-contained vessel of the egg.

readings.text: De Jong traces the motto to the pronouncement of Balgus in the Turba Philosophorum, where the old man must be fixed to the tree in celestial dew to be rejuvenated. She identifies this as an allegory for the volatile spirit descending upon and renewing the fixed philosophical body, drawing on the Pseudo-Lullian tradition of argent vive as prima materia.

commentary.title: Philosophical Egg
commentary.body: Maier uses the philosophical egg in Emblem VIII as the sealed vessel within which the prima materia undergoes transformation, requiring careful regulation of heat. De Jong interprets the egg as Maier's image for the unity of all opposites before differentiation, a microcosm of the entire alchemical process contained in a single figure.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The sealed vessel (often egg-shaped) containing the prima materia, maintained at gentle heat to incubate the Stone—the alchemical equivalent of the womb or nest.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The protected healing environment; the carefully controlled conditions of temperature, moisture, and rest that allow the body's natural restorative powers to operate.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The enclosed space of contemplation and inner work; the hermetically sealed container of the psyche in which transformation gestates before hatching into new life.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The cosmic egg of Orphic and Hermetic cosmogony: the primordial vessel from which the differentiated cosmos emerges, containing all potentialities in compressed form.

commentary.title: Vas Hermeticum
commentary.body: Maier figures the sealed vessel through the philosophical egg of Emblem VIII and the enclosed spaces where transformations occur throughout the sequence. De Jong identifies the vas hermeticum as the operational prerequisite for the entire Work, since only a perfectly sealed system can prevent the loss of volatile spirits during heating and dissolution.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The hermetically sealed vessel in which the entire opus takes place; it must be perfectly sealed so that no spirit escapes—Maier's glass house that must be well closed.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The body itself as the vessel of healing: the patient's constitution that must be sealed against external corruption while internal transformative processes complete their work.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The contemplative enclosure of the soul; the disciplined inner space of meditation and practice in which psychic transformation can proceed without dissipation.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The cosmos itself as God's sealed vessel: the bounded universe within which all celestial and terrestrial processes unfold according to the divine plan.

motto.la: Arbori affige seni in rore caelesti inclusam, et senex juvenis fiet
motto.en: Fix the old man to the tree in the garden of the dew, and the old man becomes young again.

epigram.en:
Fix the old man to the tree
In the garden of celestial dew,
And the old man will become young again,
Rejuvenated by the moisture from above.
The tree gives its fruit to him who tends it,
And the aged one grows young with the tree.

emblem-09.discourse: Maier argues that the old man represents the fixed, aged substance of the philosophical body that must be rejuvenated through exposure to celestial dew — the volatile, purifying spirit descending from above. He develops a parallel between this image and classical accounts of rejuvenation through divine intervention, including the myth of Aeson restored to youth by Medea. The discourse emphasizes that the tree functions as the apparatus of fixation: the old body is held in place while the volatile moisture penetrates and renews it. Maier cites the Turba Philosophorum and the pronouncement of Balgus as authorities for this doctrine of rejuvenation through the marriage of fixed and volatile.
emblem-09.image_description: An old man, stooped with age, is fastened or bound to a tree in what appears to be a garden or orchard. Dew or moisture descends from above — sometimes depicted as rain or celestial drops — onto the old man's body. The garden setting is lush, suggesting the dew is a life-giving rather than punishing element. The tree to which the old man is fixed may bear fruit, connecting the scene to ideas of renewal and harvest.

motto.la: Da ignem igni, Mercurium Mercurio, et sufficit tibi
motto.en: Give fire to fire, Mercury to Mercury, and that is enough for you.

epigram.en:
You want to know the reason why so many poets sing of Helicon,
And say that everybody must try to reach the top of it?
At its summit a Stone has been placed as a souvenir,
The Stone that was devoured and spat out by Saturn.
Give fire to fire, Mercury to Mercury,
And that is enough for you.

emblem-10.discourse: Maier develops the principle that like produces like: fire must be added to fire, and mercury to mercury, for the philosophical work to succeed. He argues against the common error of mixing incompatible substances, insisting that the alchemist must recognize the common nature hidden beneath different appearances. The discourse draws on the allegory of Saturn devouring his children, which Maier interprets as the dissolution of metals back into their mercurial prima materia. He cites the Turba Philosophorum's dictum that the Stone is nourished only by its own kind, establishing the principle of philosophical homogeneity that governs the entire citrinitas stage.
emblem-10.image_description: Two fires burn in separate vessels or furnaces, with a figure tending them or directing material between them. Mercury — possibly depicted as a caduceus-bearing figure or as liquid quicksilver — appears in duplicate, being passed from one vessel to another. The composition emphasizes doubling and correspondence: fire feeds fire, mercury feeds mercury, in a self-reinforcing cycle.

motto.la: Dealbate Latonam et rumpite libros
motto.en: Make Latona white and tear up the books.

epigram.en:
Only one thing of little value is found in the world,
Which is the key to the whole Work.
Make Latona white and tear up the books,
That your heart may not be rent asunder.
For knowledge without practice is worth nothing;
Practice without knowledge stumbles in darkness.

emblem-11.discourse: Maier commands two simultaneous actions: whiten Latona and tear up the books. He develops Latona as a figure for the imperfect philosophical body — an alloy of Sol and Luna stained with black impurities — that must be purified through the albedo. De Jong traces the name Latona to 'laton,' meaning electrum or yellow silver, connecting the mythological goddess to the metallurgical process of whitening a dark alloy. The instruction to destroy books signals Maier's insistence that neither theory alone nor book-learning can substitute for practical laboratory work — the alchemist must act on matter directly, not merely read about it. The discourse argues that both intellect and manual labor are necessary, but that practice takes precedence.
emblem-11.image_description: A female figure identified as Latona stands at center, her skin darkened or stained, while attendants or alchemists work to wash or whiten her body. Books or scrolls lie torn or scattered on the ground around her, their destruction commanded by the motto. The scene combines the act of purification — making Latona white — with the rejection of textual authority in favor of direct practice.

She demonstrates that 'Latona' derives from 'laton' (electrum or yellow silver), connecting the mythological goddess to the albedo stage of transmutation from black lead through transitional stages to white silver and ultimately red gold.

motto.la: Lapis quem Saturnus devoravit, pro Jove filio, eum vomitu rejecit, pro monumento in Helicone mortalibus positus est
motto.en: Make Latona white and tear up the books.

epigram.en:
Make Latona white and tear up the books,
So that your hearts may not be torn apart;
For she who is bright-skinned is whiter in the Stone,
And out of white lead originates red lead,
Which is the beginning and the end.
Without this process, the art is in vain.

emblem-12.discourse: Maier continues the argument of Emblem XI, now emphasizing the bewildering variety and obscurity of alchemical writings as the reason books must be abandoned. He argues that the sheer volume of contradictory texts drives seekers to despair, and that the only path forward is direct engagement with the material. The discourse develops the Latona allegory further: she is an impure body of mixed Sol and Luna that must be found in a humble place, immersed in dung where she becomes white lead, from which red lead originates. Maier presents this as the beginning and end of the opus — the albedo whitening that initiates the final reddening toward the rubedo.
emblem-12.image_description: The composition closely parallels Emblem XI: the figure of Latona appears again in the process of being whitened, while books and scrolls are visibly torn or discarded. The emphasis shifts slightly to the completed act of purification — Latona is lighter or whiter than in the previous emblem, suggesting progress in the albedo. The torn books lie definitively abandoned on the ground.

commentary.body: Maier references the concept of a universal solvent capable of dissolving even gold within the broader dissolution imagery of Atalanta Fugiens. registers.label: in the body
registers.text: A corrosive remedy of extreme potency, used in minute doses to dissolve calcified obstructions that milder treatments cannot address.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The supreme solvent of ego: a crisis or ordeal so powerful it dissolves even the most fixed and defended aspects of the personality.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The primordial deluge or universal solvent; the catastrophic dissolution that reduces even the most permanent cosmic structures to their elements.

motto.la: Aes philosophorum hydropicum est, et vult lavari septies in flumine, ut Naaman leprosus in Jordane
motto.en: The ore of the philosophers is dropsical and wants to be washed seven times in the river, just as Naaman the leper washed in the Jordan.

epigram.en:
The ore of the philosophers is dropsical
And wants to be washed seven times in the river,
Just as Naaman the leper washed in the Jordan.
Then the leprosy departs, and the body becomes clean,
As white as snow, more precious than gold,
If you understand what the wise men mean.

emblem-13.discourse: Maier draws on the biblical story of Naaman the leper, healed by washing seven times in the Jordan, as an allegory for the purification of the philosophical ore. He argues that the 'dropsical' stone — swollen with impurities — must undergo repeated washing to be cleansed, just as Naaman's leprosy was cured only through sevenfold immersion. The discourse connects this to the albedo purification and to the sacramental symbolism of baptism as a prefiguration of alchemical cleansing. Maier cites the Clangor Buccinae as the source of the dropsical ore metaphor, linking it explicitly to the Latona-whitening sequence of the preceding emblems.
emblem-13.image_description: A male figure, possibly identified as Naaman the Syrian, stands immersed in a river — the Jordan — up to his waist or chest. His skin appears spotted or discolored, indicating the leprosy or 'dropsy' of the motto. Attendants or witnesses stand on the riverbank observing the ritual washing. The landscape includes trees and possibly a distant city, situating the scene in a biblical geography.

motto.la: Hic est Draco caudam suam devorans
motto.en: This is the dragon that devours its own tail.

epigram.en:
This is the dragon that devours its own tail,
The serpent of the philosophers,
Which bites itself and generates itself,
Dissolving and coagulating itself.
A serpent that devours another serpent becomes a dragon;
This is the secret of the wise.

emblem-14.discourse: Maier develops the ancient image of the serpent devouring another serpent to become a dragon, an allegory for the dissolution of one metallic substance by another of similar but more active nature. He argues that in antiquity the serpent represented both poison and medicine — the pharmakon — and that the alchemical dragon born from this mutual consumption combines the properties of both parents. The discourse cites classical accounts of dragon-generation and connects them to the Hermetic principle that the Stone is produced when like consumes like. Maier emphasizes that this is a nigredo operation: the death of both serpents precedes the birth of the more powerful dragon.
emblem-14.image_description: A serpent coils upon itself, its jaws clamped around its own tail in the classic ouroboros form. A second serpent approaches or confronts the first, and the scene suggests one devouring the other in a transformative act. The setting is sparse — a rocky or barren ground — focusing attention on the intertwined, self-consuming bodies of the serpents.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong identifies the motto source in the Clangor Buccinae and traces the discourse's discussion of Mercury's distillation processes to the same text. She demonstrates how Maier connects the potter's craft of working with wet and dry materials to the alchemical manipulation of mercurial and sulphurous components through successive stages.

De Jong (1969) traces the winged and wingless bird motif of Emblem VII directly to Senior's text, where the two birds represent the volatile (Mercury) and fixed (Sulphur) principles that must be bonded despite their contrasting natures. sources.name: Lambsprinck, De Lapide Philosophico
sources.gloss: Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico is a late sixteenth-century alchemical emblem book that pairs symbolic engravings with verse explanations, establishing a visual tradition of alchemical emblems upon which Maier builds. De Jong (1969) and Pagel (1973) both identify Lambsprinck as a prototype for Maier's method of encoding alchemical doctrine in pictorial form, with Emblem VII's winged and wingless bird imagery drawing on a shared symbolic vocabulary. Lambsprinck's work thus represents a key link in the genealogy of the alchemical emblem tradition that culminates in Atalanta Fugiens.

motto.la: Opus figuli, consistens in sicco et humido, te doceat
motto.en: Let the work of the potter, consisting of dry and wet, teach you.

epigram.en:
Let the work of the potter, consisting of dry and wet, teach you.
He moistens the clay with water,
Shapes it with his hands upon the wheel,
Then dries it in the sun and fires it in the kiln.
So should you work with your substance:
Moisten, shape, dry, and fire.

emblem-15.discourse: Maier presents the potter's craft as a model for the alchemical work, arguing that the artisan who shapes clay from wet and dry elements teaches the principles governing the philosophical operation. He develops the analogy between the potter's sequence — moistening, forming, drying, firing — and the alchemist's manipulation of the mercurial and sulphurous components through successive stages. The discourse emphasizes that Nature provides the model, but art must apply it: the potter does not invent the properties of clay but learns to work with them. Maier cites this as evidence that alchemical skill is a techne learned through observation of natural processes.
emblem-15.image_description: A potter sits at his wheel in a workshop, shaping a vessel from wet clay with his hands. Around him are finished pots in various stages of drying and firing — some still damp, others hardened and glazed. A kiln or furnace glows in the background. The scene emphasizes the craft of working with wet and dry materials, the potter's hands mediating between the liquid and solid states.

motto.la: Hic Leo pennas habet quas alter non habet
motto.en: The feathers one lion has not, the other has.

epigram.en:
Two lions engage in battle:
One has wings, the other has none.
The winged one is volatile and swift,
The wingless one is fixed and strong.
Unite them, and from their conjunction
The Stone of the philosophers is born.

emblem-16.discourse: Maier develops the two lions as figures for the volatile and fixed principles of the alchemical work. The winged lion represents the philosophical mercury — fugitive, aerial, unstable — while the wingless lion is the philosophical sulphur — earthy, fixed, enduring. He argues that mastery requires capturing the winged lion and joining it to its wingless counterpart, producing a stable union of volatile and fixed. The discourse connects the lion's magnanimity in classical natural history to the nobility of the alchemical substances, and draws on the solar symbolism of the lion as the king of beasts to establish its connection to gold and the citrinitas stage of yellowing.
emblem-16.image_description: Two lions face each other in a confrontational pose. One is winged — feathered pinions spread from its shoulders — while the other is wingless, planted firmly on the ground. The contrast between the aerial, volatile lion and the grounded, fixed lion dominates the composition. The landscape behind them is open, with distant hills or mountains.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong traces the source imagery to Senior's Tabula Chimica and Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico, identifying the two lions as complementary representations of the volatile and fixed principles. She demonstrates how Maier draws on medieval and Renaissance alchemical bestiary traditions to develop the lion as a solar symbol of the citrinitas stage.
