commentary.title: Mercurius
commentary.body: Maier encodes Mercurius as the volatile, fleeing principle throughout Atalanta Fugiens, most explicitly in the frontispiece where Atalanta herself represents the volatile Mercury that Hippomenes (Sulphur) must pursue and fix. De Jong shows that the winged figures in Emblems VII and XVI consistently signify the Mercurial principle in its lunar, feminine aspect.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The philosophical Mercury: not common quicksilver but the universal solvent and volatile principle—the moist, cold, feminine component of the metallic dyad.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The vital spirit or pneuma that circulates through the body; the mercurial principle governing nerve function, respiration, and the subtle fluids.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The anima or world-soul; the mediating spirit that connects body and soul, matter and intellect—Hermes as psychopomp guiding transformation.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The planet Mercury as cosmic messenger between Sun and Moon; the principle of mediation and communication linking all levels of the great chain of being.

commentary.title: Sulphur
commentary.body: Maier consistently figures Sulphur as the fixed, pursuing principle, embodied in the frontispiece by Hippomenes who chases Atalanta with golden apples as catalytic lures. De Jong demonstrates that the wingless figures in Emblems VII and XVI represent Sulphur's solar, masculine nature, which must bond with its volatile counterpart to complete the Work.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The philosophical Sulphur: the hot, dry, masculine, combustible principle in metals—the active seed that gives form and color to the metallic body.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The vital heat or innate calor that drives digestion, growth, and generation; the choleric fire that, in proper measure, sustains bodily life.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The soul's desire and will; the active, formative principle of consciousness that shapes raw experience into meaning and purpose.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The solar and fiery principle; Sulphur corresponds to the Sun's generative heat that activates all earthly matter through its formative rays.

commentary.title: Luna
commentary.body: Maier figures Luna as the volatile, feminine counterpart to Sol, embodied in the fleeing Atalanta of the frontispiece and the winged figures of Emblems VII and XVI. De Jong traces Maier's lunar symbolism to the Senior Zadith tradition, where Moon and Sun must unite to produce the perfected Stone.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Silver in its philosophical sense: the receptive, reflective metal that must be conjoined with Sol to achieve the complete work.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The brain and lymphatic system; the cool, moist, phlegmatic principle governing the body's receptive and reflective capacities.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The receptive, contemplative faculty of the soul; the mirror that reflects divine light without generating it—imagination and intuition.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Moon as cosmic mediator between celestial fire and terrestrial water; governess of tides, menstruation, and all cyclical change in the sublunary world.

commentary.title: Sublimatio
commentary.body: Maier figures sublimation through the winged and ascending imagery that recurs across the emblem sequence, where volatile substances rise above their earthly matrix. De Jong connects this operation to Maier's hierarchical cosmology in which the Work proceeds by elevating base matter toward its celestial archetype.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Raising volatile spirits from gross matter through heat; the purified essence ascends and condenses on the upper walls of the vessel.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The refinement of crude bodily spirits into subtle vital pneuma; the upward movement of healing vapors in steam baths and fumigations.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The elevation of consciousness from base material concerns to refined spiritual perception; the ascent of the soul toward the divine.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The ascent of earthly vapors to become celestial dew and rain; the vertical axis connecting earth to heaven in the cosmic circulatory system.

motto.la: Orbis quadrifidus ignis hoc opus regit
motto.en: A fourfold fire-ball controls this work.

epigram.en:
A fourfold fire-ball controls this work:
There is the fire of the lamp, the fire of the ash-bath,
The fire of the substance itself, and the fire of water.
Four fires are needed, not one alone;
He who knows how to manage them all
Has found the key to the art.

emblem-17.discourse: Maier argues that the alchemical work requires not one fire but four distinct types, each governing a different phase of the operation. He identifies these as the fire of the lamp (external heat), the fire of the ash-bath (gentle, sustained warmth), the fire of the substance it self (intrinsic reactive heat), and the fire of the water-bath (moist, temperate heat). The discourse develops the principle that fire transforms by making things fiery — communicating its own nature — but can not make gold directly, only prepare the conditions for gold's emergence. Maier cites this fourfold fire as the master key to the practical art, without which even correct materials will fail.
emblem-17.image_description: A spherical fireball, divided into four sections or quadrants, hovers or burns at the center of the composition. Each quadrant may represent a different type of fire or heat. Flames radiate outward from the fourfold sphere. A figure — possibly the alchemist — tends or controls the fire from below. The scene emphasizes the multiplicity of fires needed and the skill required to manage them simultaneously.

De Jong (1969) traces the winged and wingless bird motif of Emblem VII directly to Senior's text, where the two birds represent the volatile (Mercury) and fixed (Sulphur) principles that must be bonded despite their contrasting natures. Emblem VII's depiction of the young bird flying from the nest and falling back encodes this teaching in Maie

motto.la: Igni naturam monstrat ignis, non aurifex auro
motto.en: Fire likes making things fiery, but not, like gold, making gold.

epigram.en:
Fire likes making things fiery,
But not, like gold, making gold.
Fire transforms what is placed within it
Into its own nature, communicating its heat.
But gold requires a different art:
Patience, knowledge, and the right degree of warmth.

emblem-18.discourse: Maier continues the fire the me from Emblem XVII, arguing that fire delights in making things partake of its own fiery nature but can not directly transmute base metals into gold. He develops a distinction between fire as agent of transformation and gold as the goal: fire prepares, purifies, and refines, but the ultimate product — the philosopher's stone or philosophical gold — emerges from the properly prepared matter's own latent potential, not from fire alone. The discourse cites the Aristotelian principle of like acting upon like to explain why the fire must be matched in kind and degree to the substance it works upon.
emblem-18.image_description: Flames or fire dominate the composition, with a figure working at a furnace or athanor. The fire burns intensely, and various alchemical vessels are arranged around or within the flames. The scene may show the figure adjusting the heat or feeding the fire. The emphasis is on the sustained, controlled application of heat as the governing principle of the work.

motto.la: Si de quatuor unum occidas, subito omnes mortui erunt
motto.en: If you kill one of the four, every body will be dead immediately.

epigram.en:
If you kill one of the four,
Everybody will be dead immediately.
For the four are bound together so tightly
That the death of one means the death of all.
Separate them gently, not by force,
Or the whole work will be destroyed.

emblem-19.discourse: Maier develops the idea that the four elements or components of the philosophical substance are so intimately connected that destroying one annihilates all. He argues that this demonstrates their essential unity — they are not truly four separate things but four aspects of a single body. The discourse draws on the myth of Geryon, the three-bodied king of Spain, and his pure-bred cattle guarded by the dog Orthrus, developing this as an allegory for the composite nature of the prima materia. Maier uses this to warn the alchemist against violent separation: the elements must be gently distinguished, not forcibly torn apart, lest the entire work be destroyed.
emblem-19.image_description: Four figures stand together in a group — possibly representing four brothers, four elements, or four aspects of a single substance. One figure strikes or kills another while the remaining two look on or collapse. The composition conveys a chain reaction: the death of one precipitates the death of all. The setting is an open space, perhaps a courtyard, with the violence at the center of the scene.

sources.name: Pseudo-Aristotle, Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis
sources.gloss: The Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis Philosophici is a short Latin alchemical treatise falsely attributed to Aristotle, transmitted through the Artis Auriferae compilation and widely known in early modern alchemical circles. sources.name: Solomonic / Biblical Wisdom Tradition (Proverbs)
sources.gloss: The Solomonic wisdom tradition, centered on the Book of Proverbs and its personification of Wisdom as a tree of life, provides the religious-philosophical foundation for the sapiential dimension of Atalanta Fugiens. sources.name: Merlini Allegory
sources.gloss: The Merlini Allegory is a medieval alchemical narrative in which a king suffering from a wasting disease is cured through a sequence of purgative and transformative operations, serving as an extended parable for the purification of base metal. De Jong first analyzed this source in his 1964 article on Emblem XLVIII and expanded the treatment in his 1969 monograph, demonstrating that Maier draws the entire King Duenech narrative from this tradition. Emblem XLVIII depicts the king accepting a curative potion, with the medical-humoral allegory encoding the alchemical process of purging impurities

commentary.title: Geryon
commentary.body: Maier invokes Geryon in Emblem XIX ('If you kill one of the four, everybody will be dead immediately'), using the three-bodied king as an allegory for the inseparability of the philosophical substance's components. De Jong traces this to the Turba Philosophorum's teaching that the Stone's elements cannot be isolated without destroying the work. Szulakowska reads the four-warriors motif as a disguised Christological resurrection allegory.

motto.la: Naturam natura docet, debellet ut ignem
motto.en: Nature teaches Nature, Nature conquers Nature, Nature rules Nature.

emblem-20.discourse: Maier articulates one of alchemy's foundational maxims: Nature teaches Nature, Nature conquers Nature, Nature rules Nature. He argues that the alchemist must learn by observing natural processes, then apply those lessons to guide and finally master the transformations of matter. The discourse connects this to Democritus's principle that art imitates nature, and extends it: the alchemical art does not merely copy natural processes but accelerates and perfects them. Maier cites the washing of dirty linen (Emblem III) as an example — Nature provides rain and sun, and the was her woman learns to replicate these cleansing agents.
emblem-20.image_description: Three female figures stand in sequence, each teaching or demonstrating something to the next. The first figure may hold a natural object, the second observes or learns, and the third applies what she has learned to overcome or master the preceding figure. The arrangement suggests a pedagogical chain: nature instructs, nature learns, nature masters. The setting is outdoors with natural elements — plants, earth, water.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong identifies the motto source in the Tabula Smaragdina and traces how Maier develops the nursing metaphor across Emblems I-II, connecting the wind (volatile mercury) as father to the earth (fixed body) as nurse. She demonstrates the systematic use of the Emerald Tablet as a structural template for the opening emblem sequence.

sources.name: Tabula Smaragdina (Emerald Tablet)
sources.gloss: The Tabula Smaragdina, or Emerald Tablet, is a brief Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus that circulated widely in Latin translation from the twelfth century onward, encoding the foundational principle that operations in the macrocosm mirror those in the microcosm. De Jong (1969) demonstrates that Maier deliberately derives the mottos of Emblems I and II from the Tabula's dictum that the earth is the nurse of the philosophical child, establishing the Hermetic cosmological framework as the opening gesture of Atalanta Fugiens. These two emblems anchor the entire work in the tradition

motto.la: Fac ex mare et foemina circulum, inde quadrangulum, hinc triangulum, fac circulum et habebis Lapidem Philosophorum
motto.en: Make a circle out of a man and a woman, out of this a square, out of this a triangle, make a circle, and you will have the Philosopher's Stone.

epigram.en:
Make a circle out of a man and a woman,
From which a quadrangular body arises with equal sides.
Derive from it a triangle, which is in contact on all sides with a round sphere:
Then the Stone will have come into existence.
If this great thing does not immediately present itself to your mind,
Learn all the doctrine of Geometry, and you will know everything.

emblem-21.discourse: Maier develops the famous geometric formula attributed to the Rosarium Philosophorum: make a circle from a man and woman (the coniunctio of opposites), transform this into a square (the four elements), reduce the square to a triangle (the tria prima of salt, sulphur, and mercury), and finally resolve the triangle back into a circle (the unified philosopher's stone). He argues that this sequence encodes the entire alchemical opus in geometric form, drawing on Platonic philosophy to connect ideal mathematical forms to material transformations. The discourse cites the principle of squaring the circle — an impossibility in mathematics but achievable in alchemy — as evidence that the philosophical art transcends ordinary reason.
emblem-21.image_description: A geometric diagram at center shows the nested transformation of shapes: a man and woman form a circle, which is inscribed in a square, which contains a triangle, which encloses a final inner circle. The figures may be rendered as human bodies contorted into these geometric forms, or as abstract diagrams with human figures at the periphery. The composition is schematic and diagrammatic rather than narrative, emphasizing the mathematical-philosophical dimension of the alchemical work.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: Rosarium formula: make circle from man and woman, derive square and triangle, return to circle. Four elements within unity. Body/spirit/soul triad.

readings.author: Hereward Tilton
readings.title: The Quest for the Phoenix: Spiritual Alchemy and Rosicrucianism in the Work of Count Michael Maier (1569-1622)
readings.text: Interprets through Aristotelian elemental transmutation: black Saturn/lead = body/earth, white phase = spirit/water, yellowness = soul/air, final redness = perfected unity of the stone. Not simply Paracelsian tria prima.

readings.author: Hereward Tilton
readings.title: The Quest for the Phoenix: Spiritual Alchemy and Rosicrucianism in the Work of Count Michael Maier (1569-1622)
readings.text: Tilton interprets the squaring of the circle through Aristotelian elemental transmutation rather than the Paracelsian tria prima. The circle-square-triangle-circle sequence represents the cosmic work from monad through elements to perfected unity, the return to the Monad.

readings.author: J.B. Craven
readings.title: Count Michael Maier: Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, Alchemist, Rosicrucian, Mystic, 1568-1622
readings.text: Craven summarizes Emblem 21: squaring the circle — make of man and woman a circle, then quadrangle, then triangle, then circle again to obtain the Stone of the Wise.

The composition is schematic and diagrammatic rather than narrative, emphasizing the mathematical-philosophical dimension of the alchemical work.

commentary.title: Maier's discourse
commentary.body: Maier develops the famous geometric formula attributed to the Rosarium Philosophorum: make a circle from a man and woman (the coniunctio of opposites), transform this into a square (the four elements), reduce the square to a triangle (the tria prima of salt, sulphur, and mercury), and finally resolve the triangle back into a circle (the unified philosopher's stone). He argues that this sequence encodes the entire alchemical opus in geometric form, drawing on Platonic philosophy to connect ideal mathematical forms to material transformations. The discourse cites the principle of squaring the circle — an impossibility in mathematics but achievable in alchemy — as evidence that the philosophical art transcends ordinary reason.
commentary.cite: Summary of Maier's prose discourse (Claudiens corpus extraction)

commentary.title: De Jong's analysis
commentary.body: Rosarium formula: make circle from man and woman, derive square and triangle, return to circle. Four elements within unity. Body/spirit/soul triad.
commentary.cite: H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems (1969), Emblem XXI section

commentary.title: Historical commentary
commentary.body: Interprets through Aristotelian elemental transmutation: black Saturn/lead = body/earth, white phase = spirit/water, yellowness = soul/air, final redness = perfected unity of the stone. Not simply Paracelsian tria prima.
commentary.cite: Hereward Tilton, The Quest for the Phoenix: Spiritual Alchemy and Rosicrucianism in the Work of Count Michael Maier (1569-1622) (2003), Discussion of Emblem XXI

commentary.title: Historical commentary
commentary.body: Tilton interprets the squaring of the circle through Aristotelian elemental transmutation rather than the Paracelsian tria prima. The circle-square-triangle-circle sequence represents the cosmic work from monad through elements to perfected unity, the return to the Monad.
commentary.cite: Hereward Tilton, The Quest for the Phoenix: Spiritual Alchemy and Rosicrucianism in the Work of Count Michael Maier (1569-1622) (2003), Ch. V, pp. 186-188

commentary.title: Historical commentary
commentary.body: Craven summarizes Emblem 21: squaring the circle — make of man and woman a circle, then quadrangle, then triangle, then circle again to obtain the Stone of the Wise.
commentary.cite: J.B. Craven, Count Michael Maier: Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, Alchemist, Rosicrucian, Mystic, 1568-1622 (1910), p. 90

commentary.body: The Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis Philosophici is a short Latin alchemical treatise falsely attributed to Aristotle, transmitted through the Artis Auriferae compilation and widely known in early modern alchemical circles. De Jong (1969) identifies it as the direct motto source for Emblems IV and V, providing both the brother-sister marriage imagery (the union of hot/dry and cold/moist principles) and the striking image of the toad suckling at the woman's breast. These two emblems draw their central conceit of elemental union through mutual transformation directly from the Pseudo-Aristotelian

De Jong (1969) shows that Maier draws from the Rosarium the geometric circle-square-triangle formula central to Emblem XXI and the sapiential-biblical framework of Emblems XXVI and XXVII, where Proverbs is accessed not directly but through the Rosarium's mediation. commentary.title: Coniunctio
commentary.body: Maier presents the union of opposites as the central mystery of the Work, depicting it through the marriage of brother and sister (Emblem IV) and the hermaphrodite figure (Emblem XXXIII). De Jong traces this theme across 14 emblems, identifying it as the structural backbone of the entire emblem sequence.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The chemical wedding of Sulphur and Mercury—the union of the red king and white queen in the sealed vessel to produce the hermaphroditic Rebis.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The rebalancing of contrary humors into harmonious proportion; the therapeutic union of hot and cold, moist and dry principles within the body.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The sacred marriage of opposites within the psyche—conscious and unconscious, masculine and feminine—producing wholeness and inner unity.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The conjunction of Sol and Luna, the great celestial marriage whose earthly reflection governs generation and the harmony of macrocosm and microcosm.

commentary.title: Rubedo
commentary.body: Maier represents the final reddening as the culmination of the geometric formula in Emblem XXI, where the return to the circle signifies perfected unity. De Jong identifies the color progression from black through white to red as structuring the entire second half of the emblem sequence, reaching completion in Emblem L.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The reddening: final stage where the white stone is tinged to red through fermentation with gold, producing the Philosopher's Stone or Red Tincture.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The sanguine temperament perfected; full vitality, robust health, and the balanced circulation of life-giving blood through the body.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The sacred marriage of soul and body achieved; full individuation, wholeness, and the philosopher's union with the divine ground.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Sun's dominion and the completion of the cosmic cycle; gold as the perfected metal reflecting the eternal and immutable light of the fixed stars.

commentary.title: Philosopher's Stone
commentary.body: Maier presents the Stone not as a single emblem but as the telos toward which the entire fifty-emblem sequence converges, with the geometric formula of Emblem XXI and the mutual destruction of Emblem L both pointing to its achievement. De Jong argues that Maier understands the Lapis as the perfected union of fixed and volatile, achieved through the complete cycle of dissolution and reconstitution.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Lapis Philosophorum: the perfected red powder or tincture capable of transmuting base metals into gold and serving as the universal medicine—the opus's ultimate product.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The panacea or universal medicine that cures all diseases, restores youth, and grants extraordinary longevity—the supreme aim of iatrochemical practice.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The fully realized self; the incorruptible inner gold achieved through the complete integration of all psychic opposites—the goal of the soul's Great Work.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The quintessence crystallized: the fifth element that transcends and perfects the four mundane elements, embodying the perfection of cosmic order in material form.

commentary.title: Rosarium Philosophorum
commentary.body: Rose Garden of Philosophers; major alchemical compilation. Source for geometric, sapiential, and washing themes.

commentary.title: Tria Prima
commentary.body: Maier's relationship to the Paracelsian tria prima is contested in the scholarship on Atalanta Fugiens. Tilton argues that reducing Emblem XXI's geometric formula to a straightforward Paracelsian reading misses Maier's deeper engagement with Aristotelian elemental transmutation and the Rosarium tradition, positioning the work within a pre-Paracelsian alchemical lineage.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Paracelsus's three principles—Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt—replacing the Aristotelian four elements as the fundamental components of all matter and the basis of spagyric analysis.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The three physiological principles: Sulphur as vital heat and combustibility, Mercury as fluidity and volatility, Salt as structure and solidity—the Paracelsian diagnostic triad.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: Spirit, soul, and body: the tripartite anthropology in which Mercury mediates between the fiery will (Sulphur) and the material vessel (Salt).

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The three cosmic principles reflecting the Trinity: the active formative fire (Sulphur), the receptive universal medium (Mercury), and the crystallized manifest world (Salt).

commentary.title: Lapis
commentary.body: Maier uses Lapis as the culminating goal toward which the fifty-emblem sequence converges, with the geometric formula of Emblem XXI encoding the method of its production. De Jong identifies the Stone as Maier's image for the perfected union of all opposites, achieved only after the complete cycle of dissolution, purification, and reconstitution.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Stone: shorthand for the Philosopher's Stone in its most general sense—the goal and product of the alchemical art, whether conceived as powder, tincture, or elixir.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The perfected medicine in solid form; the Stone as universal remedy whose mere proximity or touch is sufficient to transmute disease into health.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The cornerstone rejected by the builders; the despised and hidden treasure of self-knowledge that the world overlooks but the wise recognize as supremely precious.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The cosmic keystone; the perfected microcosmic substance that, as the Turba states, gives access to all the secrets of macrocosm and microcosm.

commentary.title: Opus Magnum
commentary.body: Maier conceives Atalanta Fugiens itself as a guide to the Opus Magnum, with the fifty-emblem sequence mapping the stages of the Work from cosmological foundation through purification, conjunction, and final perfection. De Jong argues that the deliberate ordering of emblems reflects the sequential logic of the Great Work, making the book a symbolic enactment of the alchemical process it describes.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Great Work itself: the entire sequence of operations from prima materia to Philosopher's Stone, encompassing nigredo, albedo, citrinitas, and rubedo.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The complete course of treatment from diagnosis through crisis to cure; the physician's magnum opus of restoring the patient from sickness to perfected health.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The lifelong work of self-transformation; the soul's journey from unconscious chaos through successive purifications to the gold of realized wisdom.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The divine creative act mirrored in human artifice; the alchemist's work as a microcosmic recapitulation of God's original creation of order from chaos.

commentary.title: Circulatio
commentary.body: Maier encodes circulatio in the geometric formula of Emblem XXI, where the circle symbolizes the completed cycle of operations that must be repeated until perfection is achieved. De Jong reads the circular imagery as Maier's figure for the iterative nature of the Work, where each cycle refines the matter further.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The repeated distillation and recombination of volatile and fixed components in a sealed vessel, refining the matter through iterative cycles.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The circulation of blood and vital spirits through the body; the continuous cycle of nourishment, purification, and renewal that sustains life.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The iterative deepening of self-knowledge through repeated cycles of dissolution and reintegration; the spiral path of spiritual maturation.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The great circulation of celestial influences from heaven to earth and back; the Hermetic cycle linking macrocosm and microcosm in perpetual exchange.

commentary.title: Aurum Philosophicum
commentary.body: Maier consistently distinguishes between common gold and philosophical gold throughout Atalanta Fugiens, particularly in Emblem VI where the gold sown in white earth is the seed of the philosophical rather than the metallic variety. De Jong traces this distinction to the Rosarium tradition where philosophical gold is the product of art perfecting nature.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Philosophical gold: not common bullion but the perfected seed of gold freed from material impurity—the active principle of the completed Stone.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The perfected vital essence; potable gold as the supreme medicine that restores perfect health by harmonizing all bodily processes to their ideal state.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The incorruptible core of the self; the imperishable spiritual gold that survives every trial and constitutes the philosopher's true attainment.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The solar substance in its purest form; the celestial gold that corresponds to the Sun's essence rather than its mere terrestrial reflection in mineral veins.

commentary.title: Citrinitas
commentary.body: Maier treats citrinitas as a transitional moment rather than a fully dramatized stage, and no single emblem is devoted to it exclusively. De Jong notes that Tilton reads the yellowing into the geometric progression of Emblem XXI, where the soul-as-air phase corresponds to the intermediate vivification between albedo and rubedo.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The yellowing: a transitional phase between albedo and rubedo where the white matter takes on a golden hue, signaling the approach of perfection.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Associated with yellow bile and the choleric temperament in its constructive aspect—vital heat that drives metabolism and bodily vigor.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The dawning of solar consciousness; wisdom emerging between the passive receptivity of albedo and the full realization of rubedo.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The dawn and the rising sun; the transitional moment when lunar silver yields to solar gold in the celestial cycle.

commentary.title: Hippomenes
commentary.body: Maier casts Hippomenes as the alchemical adept who must use strategy and the golden apples of Art to slow and fix the fleeing volatile principle. De Jong reads the golden apples as the catalytic agents of the Work, without which brute pursuit of Mercury would be futile, making Hippomenes a figure for the disciplined application of alchemical knowledge.

commentary.title: Cauda Pavonis
commentary.body: Maier alludes to the color transformations within the vessel across the emblem sequence, with the peacock's tail representing the intermediate moment when the black matter begins to show the full spectrum of colors before resolving into white. De Jong notes this transitional phenomenon as part of Maier's color symbolism linking the stages of the opus.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The peacock's tail: the iridescent display of colors appearing in the vessel during the transitional phase between nigredo and albedo, signaling that the matter is alive and progressing.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The crisis of fever showing many-colored symptoms—a sign that the body is actively fighting disease and that the humoral disturbance is moving toward resolution.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The dazzling but transient visions and psychic phenomena that arise during spiritual transformation; beautiful but not yet the stable light of true illumination.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The rainbow as bridge between heaven and earth; the spectrum of planetary colors reflected in the alchemical vessel, recapitulating the diversity of celestial influences.

emblem-21.armature_basis: The taxonomy's proving case. The inscribed circle / triangle / square is PAINTED ON the wall: under the old pipeline it becomes a card that pops forward and detaches from the masonry, and you can walk behind Maier's central geometrical argument. It must be a decal on the reconstructed wall. The inner circle holding the coupled figures is a picture inside that picture, so it is a decal on a decal and has depth zero forever. Anything inscribed, painted, held or engraved WITHIN a plate belongs in this category, and it is the commonest misclassification in the corpus.

plate.focal_basis: ASSUMED 46 deg horizontal FOV. The wall is frontoparallel, so it yields no vanishing point at all, and the drawing instruments lying on the ground are too short to give a reliable one.

motto.la: Cum habueris album plumbum, fac opus mulierum, hoc est, COQUE
motto.en: When you have obtained the white lead, then do woman's work, that is to say: cook.

epigram.en:
Whoever wants to achieve much with little trouble
Should throw snow in Saturn's belly.
When you have obtained the white lead,
Then do woman's work, that is to say: cook.
Patience and steady warmth are all you need;
The rest Nature will accomplish for you.

emblem-22.discourse: Maier instructs that once the white lead (the product of the albedo) has been obtained, the alchemist must perform 'women's work' — that is, cook the substance with steady, patient heat. He develops cooking as the central metaphor for the post-albedo operations, arguing that the white substance must be slowly heated and matured, just as food is transformed by cooking from raw to nourishing. The discourse emphasizes patience and temperature control: the philosophical substance must simmer, not boil. Maier draws on the herms — three-forked road markers — as guides that show the way to straying travelers, an allegory for the textual guideposts left by earlier alchemists.
emblem-22.image_description: A woman works at a cooking fire or stove, stirring a pot or vessel containing a white substance — the white lead obtained through the preceding albedo operations. The domestic cooking scene parallels Emblem III's washerwoman: alchemical processes rendered as women's household labor. Kitchen implements and vessels surround her, and steam or vapor rises from the cooking vessel.

readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong traces the golden rain motif to the Turba Philosophorum and identifies Socrates as the speaker in the source text. She demonstrates how Maier connects the alchemical production of white lead to the Hermetic tradition of herms as guideposts, and how the command to 'do woman's work' (cooking) signals the transition from albedo to the sustained heating of the citrinitas.

Saturn/lead as the materia artis is the indispensable first step on Maier's alchemical ladder, connecting to Saturnus Sterculius — the god of manure, the thing of little value trampled in the dungheap.

sources.name: Lambsprinck, De Lapide Philosophico
sources.gloss: Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico is a late sixteenth-century alchemical emblem book that pairs symbolic engravings with verse explanations, establishing a visual tradition of alchemical emblems upon which Maier builds. De Jong (1969) and Pagel (1973) both identify Lambsprinck as a prototype for Maier's method of encoding alchemical doctrine in pictorial form, with Emblem VII's winged and wingless bird imagery drawing on a shared symbolic vocabulary. Lambsprinck's work thus represents a key link in the genealogy of the alchemical emblem tradition that culminates in Atalanta Fugiens.

commentary.title: Kronos / Saturn
commentary.body: Saturn governs the nigredo emblems throughout AF. Forshaw notes that Maier discusses Saturn vomiting up the stone as an alchemical myth. The allegory of Saturn in Emblem X is interpreted as the dissolution of metals back into mercurial prima materia. Saturn's planetary influence (coldness, blackness, melancholy) maps onto the first stage of every alchemical operation depicted in the series.

motto.la: Aurum pluit, dum nascitur Pallas Athena Rhodi, et Sol concumbit Veneri
motto.en: It rains gold when Pallas is born at Rhodes.

epigram.en:
When Pallas was born on the island of Rhodes,
It rained gold upon the citizens.
If you wish for golden rain in your work,
Let the sun-god join with Venus,
And from their conjunction golden drops will fall,
More precious than any earthly treasure.

emblem-23.discourse: Maier develops the mythological tradition that golden rain fell on Rhodes when Pallas Athena was born from the head of Zeus, interpreting this as an allegory for the moment when the philosophical gold descends or precipitates during the citrinitas stage. He argues that just as Athena emerges fully armed and wise from the mind of the supreme deity, the philosopher's stone appears fully potent when the right conditions are met — it is not assembled gradually but manifests suddenly. The discourse connects the golden rain to the 'golden shower' of Zeus and Danae, weaving multiple classical myths into a single alchemical reading of divine gold falling from the heavens as precipitation of the tincture.
emblem-23.image_description: Golden rain descends from the sky onto the island or city of Rhodes, where figures reach upward to catch the falling drops. At one side, a helmeted figure — Pallas Athena — emerges fully formed, suggesting her birth from the head of Zeus. The golden precipitation and the goddess's birth occur simultaneously, linking divine emergence with the descent of philosophical gold from above.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong identifies the wolf-king allegory's source in Strabo and in Basil Valentine's Twelve Keys, demonstrating that the wolf represents antimony used to purify gold from base alloys. She traces the metallurgical process of antimony refining behind Maier's mythological narrative of royal death and resurrection.

readings.author: J.B. Craven
readings.title: Count Michael Maier: Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, Alchemist, Rosicrucian, Mystic, 1568-1622
readings.text: Craven summarizes Emblem 23: gold rains while Pallas is born at Rhodes and the sun lies by Venus, connecting the birth of Athena to the alchemical rain of gold in the vessel.

sources.name: Tabula Smaragdina (Emerald Tablet)
sources.gloss: The Tabula Smaragdina, or Emerald Tablet, is a brief Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus that circulated widely in Latin translation from the twelfth century onward, encoding the foundational principle that operations in the macrocosm mirror those in the microcosm. De Jong (1969) demonstrates that Maier deliberately derives the mottos of Emblems I and II from the Tabula's dictum that the earth is the nurse of the philosophical child, establishing the Hermetic cosmological framework as the opening gesture of Atalanta Fugiens. These two emblems anchor the entire work in the tradition

De Jong (1969) demonstrates that Maier reads the footrace allegorically: Hippomenes represents the fixed Sulphur pursuing the volatile Mercury (Atalanta), while Venus's golden apples serve as the catalytic agent enabling their union. commentary.body: Golden rain descends from the sky onto the island or city of Rhodes, where figures reach upward to catch the falling drops. At one side, a helmeted figure — Pallas Athena — emerges fully formed, suggesting her birth from the head of Zeus. The golden precipitation and the goddess's birth occur simultaneously, linking divine emergence with the descent of philosophical gold from above.

commentary.title: Maier's discourse
commentary.body: Maier develops the mythological tradition that golden rain fell on Rhodes when Pallas Athena was born from the head of Zeus, interpreting this as an allegory for the moment when the philosophical gold descends or precipitates during the citrinitas stage. He argues that just as Athena emerges fully armed and wise from the mind of the supreme deity, the philosopher's stone appears fully potent when the right conditions are met — it is not assembled gradually but manifests suddenly. The discourse connects the golden rain to the 'golden shower' of Zeus and Danae, weaving multiple classical myths into a single alchemical reading of divine gold falling from the heavens as precipitation of the tincture.

commentary.title: De Jong's analysis
commentary.body: De Jong identifies the wolf-king allegory's source in Strabo and in Basil Valentine's Twelve Keys, demonstrating that the wolf represents antimony used to purify gold from base alloys. She traces the metallurgical process of antimony refining behind Maier's mythological narrative of royal death and resurrection.
commentary.cite: H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems (1969)

commentary.title: Historical commentary

De Jong (1969) demonstrates that Maier deliberately derives the mottos of Emblems I and II from the Tabula's dictum that the earth is the nurse of the philosophical child, establishing the Hermetic cosmological framework as the opening gesture of Atalanta Fugiens. commentary.title: Alchemical text referenced
commentary.body: Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico is a late sixteenth-century alchemical emblem book that pairs symbolic engravings with verse explanations, establishing a visual tradition of alchemical emblems upon which Maier builds. De Jong (1969) and Pagel (1973) both identify Lambsprinck as a prototype for Maier's method of encoding alchemical doctrine in pictorial form, with Emblem VII's winged and wingless bird imagery drawing on a shared symbolic vocabulary. Lambsprinck's work thus represents a key link in the genealogy of the alchemical emblem tradition that culminates in Atalanta Fugiens.

motto.la: Lupus Regem comedit et crematus vitam ipsi reddidit
motto.en: The wolf devoured the king, and after the wolf had been burnt, it returned the king to life.

epigram.en:
The voracious wolf devoured the king,
Then was thrown upon a funeral pyre.
In the consuming fire the wolf perished,
But the king returned to life, restored and young.
Thus through sacrifice and fire
The tincture is prepared that cures all disease.

emblem-24.discourse: Maier narrates a two-stage allegory: the wolf devours the king (antimony dissolves gold), then the wolf is burned, returning the king to life purified and renewed. He develops this as the central nigredo-to-rubedo sequence: the base, voracious substance (the wolf/antimony) must consume the noble but impure metal (the king/gold), and then the consuming agent it self must be destroyed by fire to liberate the purified king. The discourse draws on the metallurgical practice of antimony refining, where antimony sulphide is used to extract and purify gold from alloys. Maier cites this as one of the most practically grounded of all alchemical allegories, noting that the wolf's voracity is well known in natural history.
emblem-24.image_description: A wolf stands over the prostrate body of a crowned king, having devoured or killed him. In a second register or scene within the same plate, the wolf is shown consumed by flames on a pyre, and the king rises restored from the ashes or emerges renewed from the fire. The sequential narrative moves from predation to sacrifice to resurrection within a single image.

commentary.title: Putrefaction
commentary.body: Maier dramatizes putrefaction through the suffering of King Duenech in Emblem XXVIII and the death of Osiris in Emblem XLIV, both representing the necessary death of the old form before resurrection. De Jong and Wescott both identify the four-emblem King sequence (XXIV, XXVIII, XXXI, XLIV) as Maier's extended meditation on controlled decomposition as the gateway to renewal.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Controlled decomposition of sealed matter producing the characteristic black color of nigredo; the death that is prerequisite to all alchemical generation.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Analogous to the suppuration of wounds and the crisis of fever—the body's purgative destruction of corrupt matter that must precede healing.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The mortification of the old self; the necessary rotting away of prior identity so that the seed of the new spiritual life may germinate.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The universal law that generation proceeds from corruption, as in the Aristotelian cycle of growth and decay governing all sublunary nature.

commentary.title: Rex
commentary.body: Maier deploys the King figure across a sustained four-emblem sequence (XXIV, XXVIII, XXXI, XLVIII) that De Jong and Wescott identify as the Alchemical King cycle, dramatizing the sickness, death, and resurrection of the solar principle. The King's suffering and cure encode the entire Work in miniature, from nigredo through rubedo.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Red King: philosophical Sulphur, the solar-masculine principle that must be united with the White Queen (Mercury) to produce the Stone. In Emblem XXIV, the king is cured of melancholy.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The dominant vital principle or ruling humor; in Maier's allegory, King Duenech's melancholic sickness represents the imbalance that the art must cure.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The conscious will and ruling ego whose saturnine fixity must be dissolved before it can be reborn in a higher, more integrated form.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Sun as cosmic sovereign; the kingly principle of order, authority, and formative power that governs the celestial hierarchy.

commentary.title: Kronos / Saturn
commentary.body: Saturn governs the nigredo emblems throughout AF. Forshaw notes that Maier discusses Saturn vomiting up the stone as an alchemical myth. The allegory of Saturn in Emblem X is interpreted as the dissolution of metals back into mercurial prima materia. Saturn's planetary influence (coldness, blackness, melancholy) maps onto the first stage of every alchemical operation depicted in the series.

motto.la: Draco non moritur, nisi cum fratre et sorore sua interficiatur, quae sunt Sol et Luna
motto.en: The Dragon does not die, if it is not killed by its brother and sister, that is to say by Sol and Luna.

epigram.en:
The Dragon does not die, if it is not killed
By its brother and sister, that is to say by Sol and Luna.
Two must join together to slay the third;
Neither alone can accomplish the deed.
When the dragon's blood has flowed,
The golden treasure lies revealed.

emblem-25.discourse: Maier argues that the philosophical dragon — the unreformed prima materia — can not be killed by any single agent but only by the combined action of its own brother and sister, Sol and Luna (gold and silver, sulphur and mercury). He develops the myth of the Golden Fleece, where the dragon guarding the treasure must be slain before the fleece can be obtained, as an allegory for the alchemical work. The discourse cites Jason's quest and connects it to the Hermetic tradition that the Stone is guarded by a dragon that can only be overcome by substances of its own kind. Maier emphasizes that both the masculine (active, fiery) and feminine (passive, moist) principles must cooperate in this killing.
emblem-25.image_description: A dragon writhes at center, locked in combat with two figures — a male and female identified as Sol and Luna, or brother and sister. The dragon is wounded or dying but still dangerous. The male figure wields a weapon while the female restrains or applies a substance to the dragon's body. The scene takes place in a rocky, barren landscape suggesting the underground or subterranean.

commentary.title: Jason
commentary.body: Jason appears as one of Maier's three archetypes of the alchemist (alongside Hercules and Ulysses). The Golden Fleece quest is explicitly referenced in Emblem XXV, where the dragon must be killed by Sol and Luna before the treasure can be obtained. Forshaw notes that dragons guarding gold is a persistent motif connecting the Hesperides, the Golden Fleece, and alchemical imagery.

motto.la: Fructus humanae sapientiae est Lignum Vitae
motto.en: The fruit of human wisdom is the Tree of Life.

epigram.en:
In human affairs there is no greater wisdom
Than that from which arise wealth and health.
The fruit of human wisdom is the Tree of Life;
Whoever eats of it shall never hunger.
Seek this tree in the garden of the sages,
And you will find what the whole world desires.

emblem-26.discourse: Maier identifies the fruit of human wisdom as the Tree of Life it self, arguing that the philosopher's stone is the true 'wood of life' sought by sages across all traditions. He draws on Cicero's distinction between humans and animals — that only humans possess reason and the capacity for philosophical inquiry — to argue that alchemy is the highest expression of rational wisdom applied to Nature. The discourse connects the Tree of Life to the biblical Garden of Eden, the Hesperides, and the alchemical tradition of the arbor philosophica — the philosophical tree whose roots are mercury and whose fruit is gold. Maier presents this emblem as marking the rubedo: the tree has borne its fruit, wisdom has been attained.
emblem-26.image_description: A female figure identified as Lady Sapientia (Wisdom) stands beside or beneath a large tree bearing golden fruit — the Tree of Life. She may hold a book, a scepter, or extend a hand toward the fruit. The tree is abundant and flourishing, its canopy spreading over the scene. The setting is a garden or paradise landscape, suggesting Eden or the garden of the Hesperides.

De Jong (1969) identifies Lactantius as one of the sources feeding into the dense scriptural apparatus of Emblem XXVI, where the concept of wisdom as the food of the soul bridges the gap between Christian theology and alchemical practice. This patristic strand reinforces Maier's presentation of alchemy as a legitimate form of religious knowledge at the structural midpoint of Atal

commentary.title: Maier's motto
commentary.body: The fruit of human wisdom is the Tree of Life.
commentary.latin: Fructus humanae sapientiae est Lignum Vitae

commentary.title: Maier's epigram
commentary.body:
In human affairs there is no greater wisdom
Than that from which arise wealth and health.
The fruit of human wisdom is the Tree of Life;
Whoever eats of it shall never hunger.
Seek this tree in the garden of the sages,
And you will find what the whole world desires.
commentary.cite: Maier's own verse for this emblem, in translation

commentary.title: What the plate shows
commentary.body: A female figure identified as Lady Sapientia (Wisdom) stands beside or beneath a large tree bearing golden fruit — the Tree of Life. She may hold a book, a scepter, or extend a hand toward the fruit. The tree is abundant and flourishing, its canopy spreading over the scene. The setting is a garden or paradise landscape, suggesting Eden or the garden of the Hesperides.

commentary.title: Maier's discourse
commentary.body: Maier identifies the fruit of human wisdom as the Tree of Life it self, arguing that the philosopher's stone is the true 'wood of life' sought by sages across all traditions. He draws on Cicero's distinction between humans and animals — that only humans possess reason and the capacity for philosophical inquiry — to argue that alchemy is the highest expression of rational wisdom applied to Nature. The discourse connects the Tree of Life to the biblical Garden of Eden, the Hesperides, and the alchemical tradition of the arbor philosophica — the philosophical tree whose roots are mercury and whose fruit is gold. Maier presents this emblem as marking the rubedo: the tree has borne its fruit, wisdom has been attained.
commentary.cite: Summary of Maier's prose discourse (Claudiens corpus extraction)

commentary.title: De Jong's analysis
commentary.body: Central emblem of the book. Motto from Proverbs 3:18 but through Rosarium, not arbitrary biblical selection. Unusually dense scriptural marginalia. Maier foregrounds religious-sapiential basis of entire work. Links to Emblem XXVII.

commentary.body: Rozenrichter argues that hidden dryads in AF emblems represent a feminine dimension of the alchemical work concealed within the compositions. The Tree of Life in Emblem XXVI and the tree motifs in several other emblems may contain these transformed women, connecting Maier's mytho-alchemy to the Ovidian tradition of metamorphosis as a form of preservation.

motto.la: Qui Rosarium intrare tentat Philosophicum absque clave, assimilatur homini ambulare volenti absque pedibus
motto.en: He who tries to enter the Philosophical Rose-garden without the key is like a man who wants to walk without feet.

epigram.en:
He who tries to enter the Philosophical Rose-garden without the key
Is like a man who wants to walk without feet.
The gate is locked with strong bolts;
Only the prepared may enter.
Three things are needed: patience, knowledge, and labor.
Without these, the garden remains forever closed.

emblem-27.discourse: Maier argues that attempting to enter the Philosophical Rose-garden without the proper key is as futile as trying to walk without feet. He develops this as a warning against shortcuts in the alchemical work: the three 'cooking' or 'consuming' processes that occur in the human body — digestion in the stomach, refinement in the liver, and distribution through the blood — mirror the three stages of alchemical preparation that can not be by passed. The discourse grounds this in Old Testament wisdom literature, connecting the rose-garden to the Song of Songs and the Solomonic tradition of enclosed gardens as figures for hidden wisdom accessible only through proper preparation.
emblem-27.image_description: A figure approaches or stands before a walled garden containing rose bushes or flowering plants. A locked gate or door bars entry, and the figure has no key. The garden interior is visible — lush, ordered, containing the philosophical rose — but inaccessible. The composition emphasizes the barrier between the seeker and the sought knowledge.

motto.la: Rex balneat in Laconico sedens, a Pharut nigra bile liberatus est
motto.en: The king is bathed, sitting in a steam-bath, and is freed from the black bile by Pharut.

epigram.en:
The king is bathed, sitting in a steam-bath,
And is freed from the black bile by Pharut.
In the warmth of the moist vapors
The saturnine corruption is expelled.
The physicians attend him with care,
Until health returns to the royal body.

emblem-28.discourse: Maier develops the Allegoria Merlini's narrative of King Duenech, who is bathed in a steam-bath to purge the black bile that ails him. He argues that the king represents philosophical gold in its impure state, and the bath is the vessel in which dissolution occurs: the black bile is the nigredo impurity that must be expelled through gentle, sustained heat. The discourse connects this to the Merlini tradition's account of royal purification, where the king's illness is cured not by violent means but by the patient application of warm moisture. Maier cites the medical practice of therapeutic bathing as a parallel, drawing on his own training as a physician to validate the alchemical analogy.
emblem-28.image_description: A crowned king sits immersed in a steaming bath or vessel, attended by one or more figures — physicians or servants — who regulate the temperature or administer treatments. Black bile or dark fluid visibly drains from the king's body into the bathwater. The bath vessel is large and prominent, and steam or vapors rise around the royal figure. The attendant is sometimes identified as Pharut.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong identifies the steam bath allegory's source in the Processus Chemici and the Allegoria Merlini, tracing King Duenech's purification through therapeutic bathing to the medical tradition of humoral purgation. She connects the black bile (aqua foetida) to the nigredo impurity that must be expelled through gentle, sustained moist heat.

readings.text: Part of Alchemical King sequence. Saturn = Lead = Putrefaction stage. King undergoes purification.

readings.text: King in Turkish bath, purging black bile. Color progression black to red represents alchemical stages.

readings.author: Hereward Tilton
readings.title: The Quest for the Phoenix: Spiritual Alchemy and Rosicrucianism in the Work of Count Michael Maier (1569-1622)
readings.text: Tilton reads discourse 28's Duenech allegory as purification through sweating: the melancholic king enters the bath to expel impurities. Maier explains this as purification of both human and metallic bodies. The allegory connects to the Merlini tradition and Maier's own illness while writing Symbola Aureae Mensae.

readings.author: Walter Pagel
readings.title: Review of H.M.E. de Jong, Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens
readings.text: Pagel discusses King Duenech as dropsical and discoloured, presented in a Turkish bath undergoing purgation of black bile until red colour returns, representing the alchemical work's characteristic colour changes from black to red.

readings.author: C. Morris Wescott
readings.title: Atalanta Fugiens: The Alchemical King in Transformation
readings.text: Wescott analyzes Emblem XXVIII's fuga: Atalanta enters at G and Hippomenes imitates at A. The E-flat/E-natural dissonance (minor second) represents the King Duenech's sufferings during his cure from Saturnian melancholy in the steam-bath.

readings.author: C. Morris Wescott
readings.title: Atalanta Fugiens: The Alchemical King in Transformation
readings.text: Wescott identifies King Duenech in Emblem XXVIII as being cured of Saturnian melancholy in the steam-bath, connecting the medical tradition of music curing Saturnian melancholy to the double cleansing function in alchemical operations.

sources.name: Lambsprinck, De Lapide Philosophico
sources.gloss: Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico is a late sixteenth-century alchemical emblem book that pairs symbolic engravings with verse explanations, establishing a visual tradition of alchemical emblems upon which Maier builds. De Jong (1969) and Pagel (1973) both identify Lambsprinck as a prototype for Maier's method of encoding alchemical doctrine in pictorial form, with Emblem VII's winged and wingless bird imagery drawing on a shared symbolic vocabulary. Lambsprinck's work thus represents a key link in the genealogy of the alchemical emblem tradition that culminates in Atalanta Fugiens.

sources.name: Merlini Allegory
sources.gloss: The Merlini Allegory is a medieval alchemical narrative in which a king suffering from a wasting disease is cured through a sequence of purgative and transformative operations, serving as an extended parable for the purification of base metal. De Jong first analyzed this source in his 1964 article on Emblem XLVIII and expanded the treatment in his 1969 monograph, demonstrating that Maier draws the entire King Duenech narrative from this tradition. Emblem XLVIII depicts the king accepting a curative potion, with the medical-humoral allegory encoding the alchemical process of purging impurities

commentary.title: Nigredo
commentary.body: The blackening stage appears in Maier's depictions of death, putrefaction, and burial, particularly in Emblems XXVIII and XLIII. De Jong identifies these as drawing from the Rosarium Philosophorum's death-of-the-king sequence, where the darkened hermaphrodite of Emblem XXXIII signals the necessary dissolution before renewal.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The blackening stage: putrefaction and decomposition of matter in the sealed vessel, producing a foul-smelling black mass that signals the work has begun.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Corresponds to melancholia and black bile in humoral theory; the saturnine temperament whose leaden darkness must be purged before healing.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The dark night of the soul: ego-death and psychological dissolution that precedes spiritual rebirth and illumination.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: Saturn's dominion over the prima materia; the chaos and formlessness from which cosmic order must be extracted, associated with winter and the nadir.

commentary.title: Putrefaction
commentary.body: Maier dramatizes putrefaction through the suffering of King Duenech in Emblem XXVIII and the death of Osiris in Emblem XLIV, both representing the necessary death of the old form before resurrection. De Jong and Wescott both identify the four-emblem King sequence (XXIV, XXVIII, XXXI, XLIV) as Maier's extended meditation on controlled decomposition as the gateway to renewal.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: Controlled decomposition of sealed matter producing the characteristic black color of nigredo; the death that is prerequisite to all alchemical generation.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: Analogous to the suppuration of wounds and the crisis of fever—the body's purgative destruction of corrupt matter that must precede healing.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The mortification of the old self; the necessary rotting away of prior identity so that the seed of the new spiritual life may germinate.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The universal law that generation proceeds from corruption, as in the Aristotelian cycle of growth and decay governing all sublunary nature.

commentary.title: King Duenech
commentary.body: Maier uses the figure of King Duenech in Emblems XXVIII and XLVIII to dramatize the alchemical process as a medical cure, in which the king's melancholic illness (black bile, dropsy) requires purging through steam and potion. De Jong's 1964 article traces this figure to the Merlini allegory, while Pagel emphasizes the three-level physiological correspondence between the king's cure and metallurgical coctions.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The melancholic king of the Turba Philosophorum who must be cured in the steam bath: an allegory of the base metal requiring dissolution and purification to yield its hidden gold.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The paradigmatic melancholic patient: his saturnine excess of black bile must be treated with moist heat (the steam bath) to restore humoral equilibrium.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The soul imprisoned by saturnine depression; the leaden weight of acedia that can only be lifted through the warmth of spiritual practice and purgative ordeal.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: Saturn's influence made flesh: the heavy, cold, dry principle that must be warmed and moistened by solar and lunar forces to participate in cosmic harmony.

commentary.title: Aqua Vitae
commentary.body: Maier invokes the water of life in connection with the curative and restorative operations depicted in the King Duenech sequence, where the sick king is restored through liquid medicines. De Jong traces Maier's aqua vitae imagery to the Turba Philosophorum and the Rosarium tradition, where mercurial water serves as both solvent and elixir.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The water of life: a purified distillate—often the philosophical mercury in its most refined form—capable of reviving dead metals and perfecting the Stone.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The quintessence extracted from wine or herbs; a life-giving elixir believed to restore vitality, extend life, and cure otherwise fatal diseases.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The living water of divine grace; the spiritual nourishment that sustains the soul through the arid phases of the Great Work.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The celestial dew or astral moisture that descends from the stars to vivify all terrestrial life; the subtle medium through which cosmic influences operate.

commentary.title: Rex
commentary.body: Maier deploys the King figure across a sustained four-emblem sequence (XXIV, XXVIII, XXXI, XLVIII) that De Jong and Wescott identify as the Alchemical King cycle, dramatizing the sickness, death, and resurrection of the solar principle. The King's suffering and cure encode the entire Work in miniature, from nigredo through rubedo.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The Red King: philosophical Sulphur, the solar-masculine principle that must be united with the White Queen (Mercury) to produce the Stone. In Emblem XXIV, the king is cured of melancholy.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: The dominant vital principle or ruling humor; in Maier's allegory, King Duenech's melancholic sickness represents the imbalance that the art must cure.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The conscious will and ruling ego whose saturnine fixity must be dissolved before it can be reborn in a higher, more integrated form.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The Sun as cosmic sovereign; the kingly principle of order, authority, and formative power that governs the celestial hierarchy.

commentary.title: Aqua Regia
commentary.body: Maier references the concept of a universal solvent capable of dissolving even gold within the broader dissolution imagery of Atalanta Fugiens. De Jong connects this to the alchemical paradox that the most noble substance requires the most powerful agent of destruction before it can be reconstituted in perfected form.

registers.label: in the laboratory
registers.text: The royal water: a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold—the only solvent powerful enough to attack the noblest metal.

registers.label: in the body
registers.text: A corrosive remedy of extreme potency, used in minute doses to dissolve calcified obstructions that milder treatments cannot address.

registers.label: in the soul
registers.text: The supreme solvent of ego: a crisis or ordeal so powerful it dissolves even the most fixed and defended aspects of the personality.

registers.label: in the heavens
registers.text: The primordial deluge or universal solvent; the catastrophic dissolution that reduces even the most permanent cosmic structures to their elements.

motto.la: Ut Salamandra vivit igne sic et Lapis
motto.en: Just as the Salamander lives in the fire, so also the Stone.

epigram.en:
Just as the Salamander lives in the fire
And is not consumed by the flames,
So also the Stone endures the test of fire,
Growing stronger where other things perish.
What fire cannot destroy is truly fixed;
This is the mark of the perfected substance.

emblem-29.discourse: Maier develops the ancient belief that the salamander lives in fire without being consumed, applying it as an allegory for the philosopher's stone, which endures the test of fire and emerges unchanged or improved. He argues that just as the salamander is nourished rather than destroyed by flames, the perfected stone with stands any degree of heat — a key test of its authenticity. The discourse connects this to the broader principle of fixation: a substance is 'fixed' when it can endure fire without volatilizing. Maier cites classical natural historians including Pliny on the salamander's fire-resistance, while noting that the philosophical salamander transcends the merely natural creature.
emblem-29.image_description: A salamander sits calmly within flames, unharmed by the fire that surrounds it. The fire burns vigorously — depicted with detailed, curling flames — but the creature rests at ease in the center. The scene may include a furnace or hearth as the fire's source. The salamander's composure within the destructive element is the focal point of the composition.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong traces the salamander-in-fire motif to Avicenna's Tractatulus de Alchimia, identifying the philosophical stone's fire-resistance as the key test of successful fixation. She connects the coral analogy (growing soft underwater, hardening in air) to the same principle of state-change from fluid process to solid product.

readings.author: J.B. Craven
readings.title: Count Michael Maier: Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, Alchemist, Rosicrucian, Mystic, 1568-1622
readings.text: Craven summarizes Emblem 29: as the Salamander lives in fire, so does the Stone — the Philosopher's Stone is born in perpetual fire and stands in equal heat with the Salamander.

sources.name: Pseudo-Aristotle, Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis
sources.gloss: The Tractatulus de Practica Lapidis Philosophici is a short Latin alchemical treatise falsely attributed to Aristotle, transmitted through the Artis Auriferae compilation and widely known in early modern alchemical circles. De Jong (1969) identifies it as the direct motto source for Emblems IV and V, providing both the brother-sister marriage imagery (the union of hot/dry and cold/moist principles) and the striking image of the toad suckling at the woman's breast. These two emblems draw their central conceit of elemental union through mutual transformation directly from the Pseudo-Aristotelian

sources.name: Senior Zadith (Muhammad ibn Umail), Tabula Chimica
sources.gloss: The Tabula Chimica is a Latin translation of an alchemical work by the tenth-century Arabic author Muhammad ibn Umail, known in the Latin West as Senior Zadith, whose visionary imagery profoundly influenced medieval and early modern alchemical symbolism. De Jong (1969) traces the winged and wingless bird motif of Emblem VII directly to Senior's text, where the two birds represent the volatile (Mercury) and fixed (Sulphur) principles that must be bonded despite their contrasting natures. Emblem VII's depiction of the young bird flying from the nest and falling back encodes this teaching in Maie

sources.name: Lambsprinck, De Lapide Philosophico
sources.gloss: Lambsprinck's De Lapide Philosophico is a late sixteenth-century alchemical emblem book that pairs symbolic engravings with verse explanations, establishing a visual tradition of alchemical emblems upon which Maier builds. De Jong (1969) and Pagel (1973) both identify Lambsprinck as a prototype for Maier's method of encoding alchemical doctrine in pictorial form, with Emblem VII's winged and wingless bird imagery drawing on a shared symbolic vocabulary. Lambsprinck's work thus represents a key link in the genealogy of the alchemical emblem tradition that culminates in Atalanta Fugiens.

motto.la: Sol indiget Luna, ut Gallus Gallina
motto.en: The Hermaphrodite, lying in darkness like a dead man, needs fire.

epigram.en:
The Hermaphrodite, lying in darkness like a dead man,
Needs fire to be brought back to life.
Without warmth, the joined substance lies inert;
With it, the union stirs and breathes.
Born of two mountains, of Mercury and Venus,
The Rebis awaits the alchemist's art.

emblem-30.discourse: Maier argues that the Hermaphrodite — the unified philosophical substance combining masculine and feminine principles — lies inert in darkness until awakened by fire. He develops this as an allegory for the transition from nigredo (the death-like darkness) to the active stages of the work: the combined substance has been successfully joined but remains dormant until heat reactivates it. Drawing on the myth of the Hermaphrodite born from the two mountains of Mercury and Venus, Maier connects the figure to Morienus's teaching that the Rebis (the 'two-thing') is found not in books but through living masters. The discourse frames the Hermaphrodite as the philosophical Mercury's two-topped Parnassus, where Apollo and the Muses reside.
emblem-30.image_description: A figure with both male and female characteristics — the Hermaphrodite or Rebis — lies in darkness, motionless as if dead, upon a bed or bier. The surrounding space is black or deeply shadowed. A fire or torch approaches from one side, about to illuminate and revive the prostrate figure. The Hermaphrodite's dual-gendered body is visible, combining male and female attributes in a single form.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong identifies the source in the Rosarium Philosophorum's account of the Rebis, connecting the Hermaphrodite born of two mountains (Mercury and Venus) to Morienus's teaching that the substance must be found through living masters rather than books. She traces the two-topped Parnassus allegory to the philosophical Mercury's dual nature.

motto.la: Rex natans in mari, clamans alta voce: Qui me eripiet, ingens praemium habebit
motto.en: The king, swimming in the sea, calling in a loud voice: He who saves me will receive a great reward.

epigram.en:
The king, on whose head the crown pressed heavily,
Swims in the wide sea and continually cries:
He who saves me will receive a great reward.
If you can rescue the king from the deep,
He will repay you many times over;
For the stone multiplies in the hands of the worthy.

emblem-31.discourse: Maier recounts the allegory of the king swimming in the sea who cries out that whoever saves him will receive a great reward. He develops this as a figure for philosophical gold dissolved in the mercurial sea — the noble substance submerged in the volatile solvent, needing to be rescued through fixation. The discourse argues that the king's promise of reward represents the multiplication of the stone: whoever successfully extracts and fixes the dissolved gold will be repaid many times over. Maier connects this to the broader tradition of the 'vegetable stone' that grows and multiplies like a living thing once properly fixed and nourished.
emblem-31.image_description: A crowned king struggles in ocean waves, his head and arms above the surface, calling out for rescue. His crown identifies him as royalty even in distress. From the shore or from a boat, a figure reaches toward the king or prepares to pull him from the water. The sea is rough, with whitecaps, and the landscape behind shows a rocky coastline.

readings.author: H.M.E. de Jong
readings.title: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens: Sources of an Alchemical Book of Emblems
readings.text: De Jong traces the king-in-the-sea allegory to the Rosarium Philosophorum and identifies the 'vegetable stone' that grows and multiplies as the product of successful fixation. She connects the king's promise of reward to the alchemical doctrine of multiplication — whoever rescues the dissolved gold will receive manifold return.

readings.author: C. Morris Wescott

readings.text: Wescott analyzes Emblem XXXI's fuga: the consistent E-flat and B-flat centered on D indicate the Phrygian mode (violence), while stately half-notes shifting to rapid quarter notes musically depict the King's cry for help as he drowns. All three voices are treble, denying stability.

readings.text: Wescott notes Emblem XXXI's King wears a unique crown studded with gems and topped by five tri-lobes, distinct from all other King images in AF, serving as identification for the wise rescuer.

motto.la: Ut corallus in aquis crescit, et in aere durescit, sic et Lapis
motto.en: As coral grows under water and, exposed to the air, gets hard, so also the Stone.

epigram.en:
As coral grows underwater,
Soft and plant-like in the liquid depths,
And exposed to the air gets hard as stone,
So also the substance of the philosophers:
Fluid in the vessel during preparation,
It solidifies into the permanent Stone.

emblem-32.discourse: Maier draws on the natural history of coral — soft and plant-like under water but hardening to stone when exposed to air — as an analogy for the philosopher's stone, which is fluid and mutable during preparation but becomes fixed and permanent once complete. He argues that this natural transformation demonstrates the possibility of a substance changing its fundamental state without losing its essential nature. The discourse connects coral's petrifaction to the alchemical fixation process, where the volatile philosophical substance 'hardens' through exposure to air (the volatile spirit) just as coral solidifies above the water line. Maier cites this as evidence that the rubedo — the final reddening — involves a transition from fluid process to solid product.
emblem-32.image_description: A branch of coral grows underwater, depicted in its natural marine setting with fish and sea creatures nearby. In a second register, the same coral is shown above the waterline, where it has hardened into a rigid, stone-like form. The contrast between the soft, underwater growth and the hard, aerial solid captures the transformation from liquid to fixed.

sources.name: Merlini Allegory
sources.gloss: The Merlini Allegory is a medieval alchemical narrative in which a king suffering from a wasting disease is cured through a sequence of purgative and transformative operations, serving as an extended parable for the purification of base metal. De Jong first analyzed this source in his 1964 article on Emblem XLVIII and expanded the treatment in his 1969 monograph, demonstrating that Maier draws the entire King Duenech narrative from this tradition. Emblem XLVIII depicts the king accepting a curative potion, with the medical-humoral allegory encoding the alchemical process of purging impurities
